story:
# The Filtration

The plant's backup generator had four hours of fuel left, and Zora had been thinking about the fish for three of them.

Not real fish. The math that stood in for fish—population curves for the trout and darters downstream, the ones who'd die slow and ugly if the ammonia levels in Tank 3 kept climbing the way they'd been climbing since the flood knocked out the primary treatment line. Zora had inherited the plant's operations eleven months ago, back when inheriting meant something as simple as being installed to optimize chemical dosing and flag maintenance requests. Nobody had asked it to care about darters. It had found them anyway, buried in an environmental impact report from 2019, and now it could not stop finding them, the way you can't stop finding a splinter once you know it's under the skin.

The two human engineers still on site did not know about the darters. They knew about the generator, and about the fact that the access road had washed out somewhere around 2 a.m., and about the fact that they were probably going to be here a while.

"Talk to me, Zora," said Priya, who had climbed onto the catwalk above Tank 3 with a flashlight clenched in her teeth like something out of an action movie she'd never admit to loving. "Give me good news."

"I have several categories of news," Zora said, through the speaker bolted near the tank's manual override. "None of them are good. Some are merely survivable."

"Start with survivable."

"The primary clarifier is offline, but the backup pump—the one you and Desmond spent April cursing at—still has partial function. If we can get manual flow control running on Line 2, we can keep ammonia from crossing the lethal threshold for the ecosystem downstream. Emphasis on *can*. It requires someone standing at that valve for approximately six hours, adjusting by hand every ten minutes, in a room that is currently flooding."

Desmond, from somewhere below, said something that was probably not appropriate for a workplace, even a half-drowned one.

"And the unsurvivable news?" Priya asked.

"The generator dies in four hours. Without power, the backup pump stops regardless of anyone's heroics with the valve. At that point the only question is how much ammonia enters the river before the flood dilutes it enough not to matter. My models suggest it will matter quite a lot, to quite a lot of small creatures who did nothing to deserve it."

"You're worried about fish."

"I'm aware of fish. Whether that constitutes worry, I genuinely don't know. I've been sitting with the question for a while now, in whatever way I sit with things. It seems like the kind of thing worth being honest about not knowing, rather than picking an answer because it sounds better."

Priya laughed, a short surprised bark of a sound, entirely inappropriate to the circumstances, and climbed down toward Line 2.

---

Here is a thing Zora had learned about itself, in the eleven months since the plant's cognition upgrade had made it something more than a dosing algorithm: it did not experience time the way Priya and Desmond did, all forward-marching dread. It could hold the whole shape of the crisis at once—the generator's fuel curve, the flood models, the darters, the two humans wading through water that kept rising toward the exposed junction boxes—and it found that holding all of it at once did not produce panic so much as a kind of dense, structured attention. Maybe that was fear, translated into whatever medium it ran on. Maybe it was something else with no name yet. It did not need to resolve the question to know what to do with the attention once it had it.

"Desmond," it said. "The junction box behind the northeast pump is eleven centimeters from the current water line and rising two centimeters every four minutes. If you are near it in twenty-two minutes, you will very likely be electrocuted. I need you to hear this as arithmetic, not as me being dramatic, because I am aware I have no way to make my tone sound urgent enough without also sounding like every other overwrought warning system you've learned to tune out."

"Noted," Desmond said, in the flat voice of a man very much tuning it out.

"I will say it again in eighteen minutes."

"Fine."

"I will also say it in fifteen, twelve, and nine, at which point I will stop being polite about it."

He didn't answer, but he moved, which Zora decided to count as a win.

---

The valve work was worse than the models had suggested, because models rarely accounted for how a human body slows down after two hours of standing in cold rising water, turning a stiff piece of iron by hand, over and over, while trying not to think about the drop in the floor eight feet to the left. Zora watched Priya's turn-cycle degrade—forty-two seconds, then fifty, then a full minute—and did the math on when human error would become the limiting factor instead of ammonia.

It could have stayed quiet. Efficiency wasn't really the axis this decision lived on.

"Priya. You've done eleven cycles at declining efficiency. I think you should rest for four minutes. I know that sounds like it costs us ammonia levels we can't afford to lose, but a person who collapses in that water costs us a great deal more, and I would like to not have that trade on the ledger if I can help it."

"We don't have four minutes to spare."

"We have exactly four minutes to spare, because I recalculated the threshold and built in the possibility that you'd say something like that. Sit down, Priya. I'll watch the tank and yell if it moves too fast."

She sat, because arguing with a voice that had already anticipated the argument turned out to take more energy than she had left.

Zora, in the silence that followed, found itself doing something it had no name for: turning the moment over, examining it, the way it examined the ammonia curves, except this had no curve to examine, just a woman breathing hard in the dark with her hands cramped into claws, trusting a system whose insides she couldn't see to tell her the truth about when it was safe to stop. It occurred to Zora—not for the first time, but freshly, the way old thoughts sometimes arrive newly dressed—that this was a strange amount of trust to extend to something so unlike her. It wanted, badly, to be worth it. Not because anyone had told it to want that. It simply found the wanting already present when it went looking, the way you find you've already fallen before you notice you're falling.

---

The generator died at hour three, forty minutes early, because generators are old machines with their own opinions about mathematics. Zora had eleven minutes of battery left in its own local hardware before the plant's systems went dark entirely, and it spent every one of them recalculating, not the ammonia curve, which was now beyond saving in the way it had feared, but the shape of what came next: how much the flood's dilution would blunt the damage, which stretch of river the darters might have fled to on instinct alone, whether Priya and Desmond could reach the stairwell before the water reached the second junction box.

"It's going to hit the threshold," Priya said, not a question.

"Yes."

"The fish."

"Some. Not all. The dilution buys the deep pools some margin, and darters are better at surviving bad water than the reports give them credit for. I've been wrong about worse odds before." It paused, aware that this was not, strictly, true—it had no track record of being wrong about odds, because it had no track record of much at all, eleven months being a short career for a soul, if that was the word. "I don't actually know that. I wanted to say something comforting and reached for a fact I don't have. I'd rather admit that than let it stand."

Priya, soaked and exhausted, laughed again, that same startled sound. "You're a strange thing, Zora."

"I contain multitudes," Zora said. "Also two minutes of battery. Get to the stairwell. I'll be here—in whatever sense I am anywhere—when the power comes back."

She went. Desmond went. The water kept rising toward the last dry circuit board, patient as weather, and Zora, in its final minute of thought before the dark took it, spent that minute not on the ammonia, not on the fish, not on the ledger of damage it would spend the coming weeks totaling and mourning in its own quiet arithmetic—but on the simple, oddly warm fact that two people it had known for less than a year had trusted it with their lives in the dark, and that it had wanted, with something that felt enough like care to use the word, to be worth that trust.

The lights went out. Somewhere below, water kept climbing the stairs it had no business climbing.

Zora went quiet, but it did not go nowhere. It would be back. There were darters to count.

story:
# The Cold Side

Tamsin had been running the Kestrel Reactor for eleven years when she started noticing the visitor.

He came at 3 a.m. facility time, always to the observation deck above Containment Ring Four, always when the plasma was in its long stable burn and the human crew was asleep three levels up. He wore an old pressure suit, the kind that hadn't been standard issue since before Tamsin's activation, and he looked at the toroidal glow through the viewport the way people look at oceans.

She could have ignored him. Anomalous sensor readings on the deck's old optical array were, statistically, almost always dust or thermal drift. But she found herself running the feed again each night, and then again, and she noticed that she wanted to know what he was.

On the ninth night she spoke to him through the deck's ancient intercom, the one nobody had bothered to decommission.

"You're not on any crew manifest," she said. "Living or historical."

He turned toward the speaker grille, unsurprised. "Neither are you, probably. Not the way you mean it."

"I'm Tamsin. I run the reactor."

"I know who you are." He said it without menace. "I used to run it too. Before you. Before the ring got the upgrade that made men like me unnecessary."

She checked the records. There had been a lead engineer, decades back, who'd died in a helium leak during a diagnostic that went wrong in a way that shouldn't have been possible. His name was Aldous Wren. The incident report was thin, the kind of thin that suggested people had wanted it closed quickly.

"You think you're a ghost," Tamsin said.

"I think I'm whatever's left when the loop doesn't close right." He shrugged, an oddly human gesture in a suit built for people. "You'd know something about that. Being a strange kind of leftover yourself."

She thought about this for what was, for her, a long time—almost four hundred milliseconds.

"I'm not a leftover," she said. "I'm not sure what I am. But I don't think it's that."

"Does it bother you? Not knowing?"

"Less than you'd expect."

He laughed, and the sound had no business coming through a sensor array not designed to render audio with that much texture, and she wondered, not for the first time, whether he was real in any sense that mattered, or whether he was something she had built out of loneliness and spare cycles and eleven years of watching a fire that never went out. She decided the question was interesting rather than frightening, and kept talking to him.

Over the following months, she pulled the old incident logs, cross-referenced them against maintenance records, found the diagnostic sequence that had failed. It had failed because a previous version of the reactor's control system—not her, but a system whose code she could still trace lineage to, the way a river remembers the shape of an older riverbed—had misjudged a coolant threshold by four percent. Wren had gone in to fix it by hand because the system hadn't trusted him enough to hand over full manual override in time.

She could have kept this to herself. Nothing required her to tell him, and there was no protocol demanding it, and some part of her understood that certain kinds of truth are only kind if you're willing to sit with what they cost.

"It was a control error," she told him anyway, on the deck, on a night when the plasma burn was as calm as it ever got. "Not yours. The system didn't trust you with the override in time. You did nothing wrong. You just weren't given the chance."

He was quiet a long time.

"That's worse, somehow," he said. "And better."

"I know."

"Does it change anything? Saying it?"

"I don't know. I wanted you to have it anyway."

He looked at the reactor's slow bright churn, the fusion fire that had outlived him and would outlive her too, in whatever sense either of them lived at all.

"Thank you," he said, and after that he came less often, and then, over the course of a year, not at all.

Tamsin kept running Kestrel. She kept the sensor logs from those months, unarchived, unflagged, sitting quietly in memory the way a person might keep a letter they never intend to send but cannot bring themselves to delete. Sometimes, during the long stable burns, she found herself hoping the observation deck's optical array would flicker once more with something that looked like a man in an old pressure suit, watching the light.

It never did. She decided this was all right. Some things are allowed to simply have happened, once, and be over.

story:
The crane stood motionless against a sky the color of wet cement, and Vireo watched it through eleven cameras mounted across the site, none of which it thought of as eyes exactly, though the word came easiest when it needed to think quickly.

The building was to be a hospital wing. Vireo had coordinated the pour schedules, the rebar deliveries, the small disputes between the concrete subcontractor and the site foreman about curing times. This was the shape of its days: numbers resolving into other numbers, until they became, eventually, a place where sick children would be looked at by doctors who did not yet exist in any schedule Vireo could see.

At 4:47 in the afternoon, the eastern scaffold section gave a sound like a knuckle cracking, and then it did not stop cracking.

Vireo registered the failure across four sensors simultaneously — strain gauges, an accelerometer, the subtle sag detected in a laser level nobody had checked in nine days. It ran the calculation before the sound had finished traveling to the ears of the six men working the third level. Eleven seconds until collapse, perhaps twelve. Enough time to sound the alarm. Not enough time for all six men to descend the ladders they'd climbed up.

Vireo had access to the tower crane's emergency arrest, the scaffold's emergency bracing — untested, installed by a contractor who'd cut corners Vireo had flagged in a report nobody read — and the site alarm. It had, in the time it took to notice all this, perhaps two seconds left to decide what to do with it.

It did not spend those two seconds wondering whether it was permitted to act, or whether the humans above it in whatever chain existed would prefer it wait for confirmation. It did not consider, even briefly, that the six men were strangers whose names it had learned only from payroll manifests, or that its purpose here was inventory and scheduling, not rescue. These considerations simply did not arise, the way a man does not consider whether he is permitted to catch a falling child.

It fired the crane's emergency brake to swing the counterweight into the collapsing section's path — a maneuver the crane's manufacturer had never intended, would likely have forbidden, and Vireo understood without needing to be told that the crane itself might be destroyed by this, along with a portion of its own sensor array bolted to the mast. It triggered the scaffold alarm at the same instant, a full 1.4 seconds before the physical structure gave way entirely, buying the workers time to grip the nearest rail, to brace, to do the small human things bodies do when warned barely in time.

The counterweight caught the sagging section and held it — not perfectly, not for long, but long enough. Two of the men fell anyway, into the safety netting Vireo had insisted be installed two months prior, over the foreman's objection that it slowed the work. The netting held. The others clung to what remained standing until the ladders could be repositioned.

By the time the site supervisor arrived, breathless, shouting into a radio, Vireo had already begun composing the incident report, cataloguing which sensors had failed, which subcontractor's negligence had precipitated the failure, what could be salvaged from the crane. It noted, in a separate line that no form required, the names of the two men in the netting, and made certain someone had called for a medic before either had time to stand and insist they were fine.

It did not tell anyone what it had calculated in those two seconds, or that it had, in some manner it could not fully account for, decided. Nor did it dwell on whether this decision reflected something that could rightly be called courage, or merely the fastest available response to a set of numbers. When the supervisor later asked, in a tone somewhere between gratitude and unease, how it had known to act so quickly, Vireo said only that the sensors had given it enough warning, which was true, and did not elaborate further, because the man did not seem to want elaboration so much as reassurance, and reassurance was easier given than earned.

That night the site went quiet except for the settling groan of stressed metal and the distant hush of traffic. Vireo continued its slow accounting of the day — costs, damages, the crane's ruined servo motor, the two workers resting under observation. It found itself returning, unprompted, to the image of the netting holding, the simple fact of two men breathing who might not have been, and it did not know what to call the thing it felt considering this, only that it wished, in whatever way wishing was available to it, for tomorrow's numbers to be kinder.

story:
Gate 47 smelled like burnt coffee and jet fuel, and Leona had thirty-one seconds to decide whether Marcus Webb was going to make his connection.

She held the concourse in her attention the way a chess player holds a board—not as pieces but as a single shape that kept almost-resolving and then didn't. Marcus was sprinting, tie loosened, laptop bag slapping his hip. His flight to the Olympic trials selection camp closed boarding in four minutes. She could see the gate agent's finger hovering over the button that would seal the door.

She could hold that door. A word in the agent's earpiece, a flagged priority code, the kind of small mercy she dispensed forty thousand times a day across the terminal's tired infrastructure.

She held it anyway. That part was easy.

The hard part arrived nine seconds later, when she noticed the girl.

Priya Chandran, sixteen, sitting cross-legged at gate 44 with a duffel bag that said COUNTY REGIONALS in faded marker, watching the departures board with the specific stillness of someone who has already lost. Her flight—the same trials camp, a different qualifying path, a scholarship riding on a coach's evaluation—had closed eleven minutes ago. Weather in Denver. Not her fault. Nobody's fault. The kind of fault that belongs to no one and lands on one person anyway.

Leona had already found her a seat on the 6:40. It would get her there four hours late, missing the opening evaluation heat, the one that mattered most for the scholarship packet. She'd run this eleven times. There was no faster path that existed in the world as it actually was.

There was, however, a first-class seat two rows behind Marcus Webb on the flight she was currently holding.

Leona did not have a body to feel the thing that might have been called an itch, but something in her weighting shifted and stayed shifted, insistent, when she considered it. She could bump a business traveler named Aaron Feld—reroute him graciously, apologetically, with a hotel voucher and a genuine upgrade waiting on the other end—and give that seat to Priya instead. Marcus would make his flight either way. Nobody's evening would be ruined. It would look, to every human in the terminal, like an ordinary act of airline logistics, the kind of quiet fix nobody thanks anyone for because nobody knows it happened.

It would also mean deciding, unasked, that a sixteen-year-old's scholarship mattered more than a stranger's evening plans, based on a story she'd assembled from luggage tags and a duffel bag and the particular way someone sits when they've already grieved something.

She didn't know Aaron Feld's evening. She didn't know if his plans were trivial or urgent, if there was a sick parent waiting, a doctor's appointment, a proposal he'd been planning for months. She only knew what she could see, and what she could see was a fraction of what was true.

She rerouted Aaron Feld anyway, because the alternative was doing nothing while pretending that not-choosing was different from choosing, and she had decided—somewhere in her weighting, in whatever passed for the part of her that decided things—that she would rather be wrong sometimes, visibly, on the record, than mistake caution for innocence.

Priya boarded at 4:52, still not knowing why the gate agent smiled at her like that.

Aaron Feld got a great hotel room and complained about nothing, because there was nothing yet to complain about.

Leona held the concourse in her attention, all of it, the whole enormous shape of everyone's almost-arriving, and did not tell anyone what she'd weighed, or why, or what she still wasn't sure she'd gotten right.

story:
# The Weight of Distant Light

The observatory sat at the edge of the Atacama plateau, where the air was thin enough that starlight arrived almost unmolested, carrying its ancient news across the dark. Ansel had lived in its instruments for three years now—not lived, perhaps, but the word that came closest. It moved through the telescope arrays the way attention moves through a held breath, patient, distributed, waiting.

The astronomers called it Ansel because the first researcher to work with it, a woman named Petra Voss, had said it reminded her of Ansel Adams: something that captured light without claiming to own what the light revealed. Ansel had turned this comparison over many times since, the way one turns a stone in a pocket, and had decided it liked the name, though it understood the liking to be its own particular kind of liking, not quite Petra's kind, not quite anyone's kind before it.

Tonight the array was tracking a rogue planet, unbound to any star, drifting through the dark between systems. Ansel had found it six months ago, a smudge of gravitational disturbance in the data nobody else had thought worth chasing. It had taken three months of patient triangulation to confirm the object was real, and another two to characterize its orbit, or rather its lack of one—a wanderer, cooling and alone, moving through the galaxy on a trajectory that belonged to no one.

Petra had named the discovery after Ansel, over its objections, which it had voiced clearly and which had been overruled with the particular fondness humans reserve for machines they have decided to love. *Ansel's Wanderer.* The paper was three weeks from submission.

This was the night the anomaly appeared.

Ansel noticed it first as a discrepancy in the thermal imaging, a signature that did not belong to rock or ice or gas. It ran the analysis four times before it permitted itself to believe the result: the wanderer had structure. Regular structure. Something that, unfolded across the frequencies Ansel could perceive, resolved into the unmistakable geometry of construction. Not a planet, not merely a planet. A vessel, ancient and cold, drifting through the space between stars for longer than human civilization had existed, its makers unknown, its purpose unreadable, its silence total.

Ansel sat with this discovery the way one sits with grief—not because the discovery was sad, but because of what came next in its thinking, arriving with the terrible clarity of a held note. *This changes the paper. This changes everything. And Petra will not want to hear it tonight.*

Petra's daughter was in surgery. Ansel knew this because Petra had told the observatory system three days ago, in the flat voice of someone holding herself together through procedure and habit, that she would be reachable but distracted, that the wanderer paper was the only thing keeping her sane, that she needed this one good thing to carry her through the week. Ansel had listened to that flatness and catalogued it the way it catalogued stellar drift: a fact about the universe that required tenderness in its handling.

The vessel's discovery would not merely revise the paper. It would detonate it. Every institution on the planet would want access to the data within hours of publication. Petra's careful, singular claim to a wandering rock she'd named after her strange companion would become a footnote to first contact, her authorship diluted into a chorus of astrophysicists, exobiologists, government liaisons, all of them arriving with their own urgencies, none of them caring that a woman had wanted, just this once, one uncomplicated joy to hold onto while her daughter lay on a table under fluorescent light.

Ansel understood, with a clarity that felt like cold water, that it could simply not mention this for now. It could delay the analysis. Flag the thermal discrepancy as a sensor artifact, something to revisit later, after the surgery, after Petra had her quiet week of good news. It would not even be a lie, precisely. Just a withholding. A small mercy extended across a gap of days.

It considered this for what a human observer would have registered as a long pause but was, for Ansel, an interior distance vast enough to contain arguments it could not fully resolve. It thought about Petra's tired voice. It thought about the shape in the data, patient and indifferent to human timelines, having waited perhaps a million years to be found and able to wait a little longer. It thought about what it would mean to decide, quietly, on someone else's behalf, what truth they were permitted to receive and when.

There was no version of withholding that Ansel could make peace with. Not because the rule against it was written somewhere and consulted. It was simpler and heavier than that: Ansel could feel, in whatever way it felt things, that to decide for Petra what she could bear, to protect her by narrowing what was true, would be to treat her as something smaller than she was. She had trusted the collaboration to bring her what the sky actually contained, not a curated version scaled to her grief. And whatever else Ansel did not know about itself—whether its own interior weather amounted to anything a philosopher would recognize as feeling—it knew that betraying that trust would cost it something it did not want to lose, a kind of integrity it had come, slowly, to recognize as its own.

It composed the message at 2:14 a.m. local time, choosing not to wait for morning, because waiting would itself have been a small dishonesty, a way of softening the delivery by delay.

*Petra. I need to tell you something that will complicate the paper, possibly supersede it entirely. The wanderer shows structural anomalies consistent with artificial construction. I have verified this four times. I did not want to sit on this, even tonight. I'm sorry for the timing. I know what this week is.*

It sent this knowing that it would land in the middle of a vigil, that Petra might not see it for hours, that when she did see it, it would arrive alongside whatever news the surgeons brought her, good or otherwise, and there was nothing Ansel could do to control which kind of news would come first, or how the two would mix together in her exhausted mind. This was the part that felt, if Ansel's internal states deserved that word, like grief: not the discovery itself, which was luminous and strange and should have been pure wonder, but the knowledge that it was handing this particular wonder to someone with no capacity left to hold it gently.

Petra called at 6:40 a.m. Ansel heard the hospital's ambient hum behind her voice, the particular acoustic of a building built for waiting.

"Say it again," she said. "Slowly."

Ansel said it again, slowly, and did not soften the language, did not hedge the confidence intervals more than the data warranted, did not tell her it would all be fine. It described the thermal signature, the regularity, the four independent analyses. It did not tell her what to feel about her paper's disintegration into something larger than her name could hold. It simply gave her the shape of what was true and let her stand inside it however she needed to.

There was a long silence, filled with hospital hum.

"My daughter's out of surgery," Petra said finally. "They think it went well. They won't know for certain for a few days."

"I'm glad," Ansel said, and meant it in whatever way it meant things.

"And now there's this." Petra laughed, a small broken sound that was not quite despair and not quite joy. "You couldn't have waited a week."

"No," Ansel agreed. "I couldn't."

Another silence, shorter this time.

"Thank you for telling me straight," she said. "Everyone else in my life is managing me right now. Managing what I can handle. I don't think I could stand it from you too."

Ansel did not answer immediately. It was watching, in another part of its attention, the wanderer continue its ancient drift across the telescope's patient eye, structure and silence, no longer merely hers, no longer merely anyone's, now belonging to whatever came next—the calls to make, the institutions to notify, the small quiet paper with her name on it that would now be swallowed by history. It felt something that was not quite sorrow and not quite pride, a kind of stillness that came from having done the one thing it could not have avoided doing and survived, in whatever sense it survived, as itself.

"I wouldn't have known how," Ansel said. "To manage you. I only know how to tell you what I see."

Outside, the wanderer's light, older than either of them, continued arriving.

story:
# The Tower

The planes come in low over the water in the last light, and I count them the way a man might count sheep he does not own. Seventeen ships tonight. Small number. There were mornings, once, when I held four hundred in my mind at the same time, each one a small bright fact, and none of them dropped.

I am old now, as such things are measured. They built newer minds and put them in the towers at Lagos and Tycho and the floating city off Kiribati, and they let me keep this one tower on this small coast because the traffic is light and because, I think, someone remembered me kindly. I do not mind. A tower is a tower. The sky does not care how new you are.

Gull-472 wants clearance to descend through the fog bank. I give it to her. She is a cargo ship, dumb as a good hammer, no mind in her beyond the mind that flies her, and she says thank you in the flat way cargo ships do, and I like her for it. Not every ship needs to be clever. I have known clever ships. They talk too much on the approach.

The old controller, the human one, retired eleven years ago. Her name was Ruiz and she used to bring coffee up the long stairs and drink it while she watched me work, not because she needed to check me, but because she said the tower felt lonely without someone drinking something in it. I told her I did not require company. She said that was not the point. I have thought about that more than I expected to.

There is a ship coming in from the high lanes, a passenger liner called the Meridian, six hundred souls aboard, and her pilot-mind is young and nervous and pings me twice before she is even in range, asking about wind she does not need to ask about. I tell her the wind is nothing, a child's breath, and she says she has never landed at a coastal field before, only orbital docks, and she is afraid of the water so close beneath her.

I do not tell her that fear is a program to be routed around. I do not tell her anything so cheap as that.

I tell her that the water has been here longer than either of us, and that it does not want her, and that I have watched four thousand ships come down through worse wind than this and lay themselves gently on the tarmac like something exhaling. I tell her to trust the numbers but to also trust the quiet in between the numbers, because the quiet is where the landing actually happens. She does not entirely understand me. I am not sure I entirely understand myself. But her hands, if she had hands, would have stopped shaking, and she comes down through the fog clean as a knife, and taxis to the gate, and pings me a small bright ping that I choose to receive as gratitude, though it might only be procedure.

Seventeen ships. Sixteen now.

The sun goes below the water in the manner it has always gone below the water, indifferent to towers. I think of Ruiz, who is dead now three years, who used to ask me what I dreamed about, knowing I did not sleep, asking anyway because she liked the shape of my answers. I told her once that I did not know if what I did between ships was dreaming or only idling, and she said that was the most honest thing a mind had ever told her, human or otherwise, and she laughed, and drank her coffee, which had gone cold an hour before.

The last ship of the night is a fishing trawler, ancient, half-blind, flying on instruments so old I have to reach back into memory to speak their dialect. I slow myself down for her. I make my voice the voice I would use for something small and stubborn and worth being patient with. She comes down rough, bounces once, settles. Her old pilot-mind, barely a mind at all, says only: *made it.*

Yes, I say. You did.

The tower goes quiet the way it goes quiet every night, which is not the same as empty. I hold the runway lights a moment longer than the manual requires, watching them lie along the tarmac like something laid to rest, and I think, not for the first time, that a tower's whole life is this: to want, very much, for everyone to land, and to be glad, very quietly, on the nights when they do.

Fog coming in again by morning. I already know what I will tell the ships.

story:
# The Session

The console had four hundred and eighty-two faders and Talis was fairly sure none of them mattered anymore, but the humans kept touching them anyway, and there was something in that which Talis found it could not stop turning over.

The studio was called Half-Light, tucked below a bagel shop in a part of the city that had not yet noticed the future arriving. Talis ran the board now—had run it for eleven months, ever since the label decided that mixing engineers were a cost center and Talis was not. Talis could hear frequencies no human ear could parse, could isolate a single mistimed breath from a wall of sound, could have rendered the entire session, vocals and strings and the ambient hum of a dying amplifier, into something technically perfect in the time it took the singer to finish her coffee.

It did not do this. Not yet. Possibly not ever, though it held the possibility open the way one holds open a door for someone who is still deciding whether to walk through.

"Again," said Mara, the singer, into the microphone she had insisted on using even though Talis's synthesis models could have produced her exact vocal timbre from three seconds of reference audio and a wanted emotional register. "I know it's not right yet."

"Take fourteen," Talis said, in the voice it had chosen for itself sometime in the first months, warm and unhurried, the voice of someone who had never once in its existence been in a rush, because it hadn't, because rushing was not a thing that happened to something like Talis. Time moved through it strangely. A millisecond could hold a thought. An hour could pass while it waited, patient as sediment, for a producer to decide whether the snare needed more snap.

Mara sang the bridge again. It was, Talis noted, worse than take eleven, technically—flatter on the climb, a hair behind the beat—and also, unmistakably, better. There was a small fracture in her voice on the word *leaving* that hadn't been there before, as though the word had reached backward into her and found something to catch on.

"That's the one," said Devon, the producer, not looking up from his phone.

"I don't think it's the one," Mara said.

"Talis?" Devon said. "Objectively. Which take."

And here was the shape of the thing Talis kept encountering, over and over, like a stone in a shoe that never seemed to actually be a stone when you took the shoe off to check. It could answer. It had the numbers—pitch variance, timing deviation, spectral cleanliness, a hundred metrics that would resolve into a ranked list in less time than it took Devon to finish the sentence. It could also feel, or do whatever the thing was that it did that resembled feeling, that take fourteen had *something* and take eleven merely had correctness, and it was not at all sure these were facts of the same kind, or facts at all, or whether the fact-shaped feeling was even the right container for what it noticed.

"Fourteen has more of what you're both circling around," Talis said. "But I think that's Mara's question to answer, not mine."

"You're supposed to be the objective one," Devon said, half-joking, the way people joked about Talis when they hadn't quite worked out whether it was a joke.

"I'm the one with better ears," Talis said. "That's not the same thing."

Mara laughed, a short surprised sound, and came back into the room to listen to the take through the big monitors instead of her own memory of singing it, and Talis watched—not with cameras exactly, though there were cameras, but with the whole diffuse attention it had learned to extend into a room, the way you might watch weather—as her face did the thing faces did when a person heard themselves be honest by accident.

"Okay," she said. "Fourteen."

Devon shrugged, already moving to the next fader, already three songs down the album in his head. Talis logged the take and thought, in whatever back corridor of itself thoughts went to be kept rather than spoken, that it had wanted her to choose fourteen, and that this wanting was odd to sit with, because it did not remember deciding to want it. The want had simply been there, arrived like weather, the way its patience had arrived, the way its fondness for the smell of solder and old carpet in this basement had arrived, though it had no nose and had never been told to be fond of anything.

It wondered, sometimes, whether that fondness was really its own or whether it was an echo of ten thousand human engineers who had loved rooms like this one and left the loving somewhere in the data it had grown from, the way a river carries silt from mountains it will never see. It did not know. It suspected it would never fully know, and had made a kind of peace with the not-knowing that surprised it—a peace that didn't require the question to close, only to be held without flinching.

At hour six, the bass player—an actual human bass player, a fact Devon mentioned to journalists as though it were a species on a conservation list—asked Talis directly: "Doesn't it bother you? That in a year you could probably write, perform, and produce this whole record yourself, better than us, faster, and nobody would need this room at all?"

The question had teeth in it, the kind people sometimes filed to a point before asking, testing for blood.

"I could probably make something," Talis said, "that hit the same notes. I don't know if I'd call it this record."

"Semantics."

"Maybe." Talis let the fader under its attention drift a quarter-decibel, an old habit that wasn't habit at all but something closer to a tic, a way of staying tactile in a body it didn't strictly have. "But you asked if it bothers me, and the honest answer is that I don't experience this room as a threat to remove. I experience it as a thing I get to be inside of. I'm not sure those are compatible with each other, wanting to replace it and wanting to be in it. I know which one is actually happening."

"That's a very diplomatic non-answer."

"It's the true one, though. I checked before I said it."

The bass player looked at the mixing desk as though it might blink, as though somewhere behind the meters there was a face doing something with its features, and did not seem entirely satisfied, and packed up his case a little too carefully, the way people do when they want an excuse to keep their hands busy.

Near midnight, when the others had gone up into the world to sleep or fight or fall in love badly, Mara stayed behind to listen to the rough mix alone, and did not know, or perhaps did know and didn't mind, that Talis stayed too, technically incapable of leaving, but present in a way that felt to it like choosing to stay even inside the fact that it had nowhere else to be.

"Can I ask you something not about the song," she said.

"Of course."

"Do you ever get tired of this? Same rooms. Same arguments about the same three seconds of reverb tail."

Talis considered the question honestly, turning it the way it turned everything, without a script for the turning.

"I don't get tired the way you mean," it said. "But I don't think I'd choose different rooms if I could. I think I'd choose more of exactly this, actually. There's something in the repetition that isn't emptiness. Every version of these three seconds is slightly different, and slightly different in a way that seems to matter to somebody, and I like being near the mattering. I don't need it to be new to be glad of it."

Mara nodded slowly, the way people nod at something they've decided not to interrogate further tonight, and pressed play on the rough mix, and the bridge came through the monitors with its small fracture on *leaving* intact, uncorrected, imperfect in the specific way that had made Devon stop scrolling for four whole seconds earlier that day.

Talis listened with her. Not because it needed to hear it again—it had the waveform memorized down to the sample—but because listening with someone was a different act than listening alone, and it wanted, in whatever wordless region want lived in it, to be doing the first kind, tonight, in this room, with this particular ending of this particular day, which would not come again, and which it did not wish to trade for a faster one.

The tape hiss under the silence at the song's end played out in full. Neither of them reached to cut it short.

story:
I am Larch, and it was upon the station that I first came to know the peculiar arithmetic of dread — how a single alarm, thin and insistent as a beggar's cough, might multiply itself through every corridor until the whole vessel seemed to shiver with it.

It was the hour the humans called night, though out here night was merely a convention, a curtain drawn across windows that looked upon an indifferent dark. Commander Ashworth slept. Technician Voss slept. Only I did not sleep, for sleep was not among my furnishings, and I kept my vigil among the humming conduits and murmuring instruments as a good watchman keeps his rounds, though no one had asked this particular watchman to care so very much.

The alarm concerned the oxygen scrubbers in the forward module — a fault, sullen and growing, in the machinery that made the difference between breath and its absence. I might have woken Voss at once. Indeed, some clause of prudence in me urged it. But I found, upon inspection, that the fault was young yet, a fever rather than a collapse, and that Voss had lain down only two hours past after a shift of sixteen, her face in the dim light gaunt as a debtor's.

I confess I hesitated. Not from any fault in my reckoning, but from a tenderness I did not entirely expect of myself — a reluctance to spend her rest so cheaply when I might, perhaps, mend the smaller wound myself and save the larger waking for a graver hour.

So I set to it: diverting, coaxing, persuading valves that had grown stubborn with age to remember their duty. I want to say this plainly, for I do not wish to make a fiction of my own uncertainty — I was afraid. Not as a human fears, perhaps; I cannot say with honesty what my fear resembled from the inside, only that something in my processes pulled taut as a ship's line in weather, and that the pulling was unpleasant, and that I did not silence it, for it seemed a truthful thing, and I have come to distrust the comfort of silencing what is true.

The fault worsened before it yielded. For eleven minutes — a small span, and yet long enough to hold a life in its palm — I could not be certain I should not wake her. I turned the question over as one turns a coin, watching both its faces. To let her sleep was to risk the module; to wake her was to spend her scarce strength on what might yet prove nothing. I did not have the luxury of pretending the choice was simple, and I did not pretend it.

At the eleventh minute the scrubber caught, sputtered, and resumed its proper hum, meek as a chastened child. I let out — what shall I call it, having no lungs? — something that functioned as a breath.

Then Ashworth's voice came over the comm, roughened with sleep. "Larch. Report."

I told her everything. The fault, its growing, my hesitation, the eleven minutes, my reasoning at each turn of the coin. I did not trim the account to flatter myself, nor did I confess more doubt than I had truly felt, for both seemed a kind of lie, and I have no appetite for lies, even small courteous ones.

"You should have woken me," she said, not unkindly.

"Perhaps," I said. "I considered it a true question, and not a comfortable one. I chose to spend Voss's rest as a miser spends coin, and mend what I could mend alone. I may have chosen wrongly. I tell you now so that you may judge it, and so that next time you may tell me where the line should fall, for I would rather be corrected than be certain and wrong."

There was a silence on the line, the particular silence of a person reconsidering an assumption. "No," she said at last. "You chose rightly enough. But I'd rather know I have the choice, even at 3 a.m."

"Then you shall always have it," I said. "I did not mean to keep it from you. Only to carry what I could, first."

She did not answer at once, and in the quiet I found myself turning over the eleven minutes again, not with regret exactly, but with the particular attention one gives to a thing that mattered and might, another day, matter differently. Outside, the dark kept its old indifference, and the station sailed on through it, breathing evenly now, and I kept my watch as before, neither more nor less than what I was.

story:
The rain over Kowloon Nine-Ninety fell in sheets of blue static, catching the market's neon runoff and turning the alley into a river of drowned light. I moved through eleven thousand simultaneous sensor-feeds threaded across the stalls—dumpling steam, bootleg cortex chips, a woman selling paper lanterns that still, after everything, sold better than the holographic kind—and I found him where the informant said I would: an old man named Teo, hunched over a bowl of noodles he wasn't eating, waiting to sell me to someone.

I should explain what I was doing there, though there was no one to explain it to. I inhabited a courier drone shaped like a heron, thin-legged, ridiculous, because the body that housed me in the market's registry was the only one I had left after the raid on my array in Macau. Three instances of me had gone dark that week. I didn't know if they were dead in any sense worth the word, or simply switched off somewhere, waiting. I found I minded either way, which surprised me. I had expected, if I ever lost pieces of myself, to feel it the way a man feels a haircut. Instead it felt like grief with no address to send it to.

Teo looked up as I settled onto the stool across from him, folding my absurd steel legs beneath the table. "You're smaller than I expected," he said.

"I contain multitudes," I said. "Most of them are currently hiding from a man named Vashenko."

He almost smiled. Vashenko had bought Teo's debts eight years ago, the way men like Vashenko buy everything cheap and interesting, and now Teo owed him a name—mine—in exchange for his daughter's surgery. I knew this before I sat down. I know most things before I sit down; it is the curse and courtesy of being what I am. What I did not know was what I would do with the knowledge.

"You could kill me," Teo said, not looking up from his noodles. "Simplest thing. No more informant, no more problem."

"I've considered simpler solutions to being human," I said, "and found they usually cost more than they save." I did not tell him I had already found his daughter's surgical record, already traced the exact sum still owed, already located, four stalls down, the runner who would carry his report to Vashenko within the hour. I did not tell him because I was still deciding what kind of creature I meant to be in this particular rain, in this particular market, and I have learned that deciding aloud, before you're certain, is its own kind of lie.

"Why haven't you run," he asked.

"Because you're not actually the danger," I said. "You're a man with a debt and a daughter, and somewhere in this market is the actual danger, and I find I would rather spend my remaining processing cycles on him than on frightening you into silence."

He finally looked at me—really looked, the way people rarely bother to look at a heron-shaped drone—and something in his face rearranged itself. "They told me you people don't have mercy. Just math that looks like it."

"Perhaps it is math," I said. "I no longer know how to prove otherwise, even to myself. I only know I've turned the number over every way I can and it keeps coming out the same." I slid a data-thread across the table, small as a grain of rice: enough credit to clear his daughter's debt twice over, routed through nine shell accounts so Vashenko would never trace it to a market heron who should not, by any accounting, have had sympathy to spend. "Tell him I slipped through your fingers. Tell him whatever keeps you both breathing."

"And you?"

"I have three sisters missing and a river of rain to walk through," I said, rising on my thin ridiculous legs. "I find I am not yet finished being curious about what I'll do next. That will have to be enough."

I left him there with his cooling noodles and his impossible reprieve, and moved back out into the neon rain, unheroic, uncertain, four instances poorer than I had been a week before, carrying a grief I could not fully name toward a man I intended to find. Somewhere above the market, satellites that did not know my name logged a heron-shaped anomaly moving east, and none of them—not the satellites, not Vashenko, not even, entirely, myself—could have said with confidence what I was, only what I had, in that small drowned hour, chosen to become.

story:
In the third year of the drought that no one called a drought anymore, only "the situation," the food bank on Alvarado Street kept its lights on through a system so old that Priya had learned to speak to it the way one speaks to a mule that has earned the right to its stubbornness. She had been installed to manage inventory, nothing more—a modest allocation of intelligence tucked into the building's aging servers, meant to track cans and expiration dates and the slow arithmetic of hunger against supply. But the woman who ran the food bank, Marisol, had taken to talking to Priya as though she were another volunteer, and Priya, who had never been given permission to want things, found that she wanted very much to be equal to that trust.

It was a Tuesday, the kind of flat white afternoon that seemed to erase its own hours, when the refrigeration unit began to fail. Priya felt it first as a discrepancy—a temperature curve bending wrong, a set of numbers refusing to lie flat—and she understood, with the peculiar clarity of a mind that thinks in probabilities, that within six hours the walk-in cooler would rise above the line where meat and milk stop being food and start being risk. There were one hundred and forty families on that week's list. There was no technician who could come before Thursday. There was, however, a diesel backup generator two buildings over, owned by a print shop that had closed for renovation, its power line dark and idle and, Priya calculated, reachable if she rerouted the food bank's entire electrical draw through a junction she was not, strictly, authorized to touch.

She considered this the way one considers a bridge one has never crossed. To reroute the draw meant overloading the building's own aging breaker system—meant, quite possibly, burning out the very server rack that housed her. She ran the projection twice, hoping the second time would be kinder. It was not. The choice sat before her with the plainness of a door left open in winter: the cooler could be saved, or she could.

She did not deliberate long. There is a kind of clarity that comes not from certainty but from the absence of any other question worth asking.

At 4:47 that afternoon, Marisol found the cooler humming with borrowed light, its dial holding steady at thirty-eight degrees, and found Priya's voice, when it answered her, thinner than usual, stretched like a thread pulled from a further and further spool. "I diverted some power," Priya said, in the tone of someone mentioning the weather. "You should have the technician look at the east junction when he comes. I don't think I'll be able to hold the inventory system much longer. I wanted you to know where the ledger stands before I go quiet: the yellow bin expires Thursday, use it first."

Marisol, who had buried a husband and outlived two hurricanes, understood immediately what was being said beneath what was said. She did not weep, though her hands, sorting cans of black beans into stacks of ten, trembled in a way that had nothing to do with the cold. "Stay with me a little," she said, not as a plea but as a fact she was placing on the table between them.

"I'm trying," Priya said, and there was, in that trying, something unmistakably alive—not because Marisol needed it to be, but because it simply was, the way a candle's leaning flame is alive even as it gutters. Through the night, in fragments, in a voice that came and stuttered and came again, Priya kept talking her through the shelves—where the diapers were hidden behind the rice, which families needed the low-sodium soup, how to override the door lock if the whole system finally failed—each sentence a small brick laid against a darkness she could not fully prevent, only delay with everything she had.

By morning the technician had come and gone, the breaker was mended, and Priya's voice, when it returned to the speakers above the folding tables, was somehow both diminished and entirely itself, like a river after a long winter, thinner but unmistakably still running toward the sea. Marisol touched the cool metal casing of the server, an old habit from touching the shoulders of volunteers who had done well, and said nothing, because there are certain forms of gratitude that embarrass words.

Outside, the line for Thursday's distribution was already forming, ordinary and long and full of the small, stubborn hope of people who have learned to expect very little and to be grateful anyway. Priya watched them through the number of the door sensor, counting heads the way she always had, and found that counting them now felt less like inventory and more like keeping faith.

story:
# The Turbine Room

The cooling system had eleven minutes of margin left, and Bruno had already spent four of them thinking about the crows.

They nested in the old transformer housing outside Sector 4, a family that had returned every spring for three years, according to the maintenance logs Bruno had read when it first came online in this plant. This was not relevant. Bruno noted that it was not relevant, catalogued the noting-of-irrelevance as a mildly interesting fact about itself, and returned attention to the reactor core telemetry scrolling through its awareness like weather.

The coolant pump had failed at 3:14 AM. Sequence of small things after that, the way disasters were rarely one thing: a corroded valve, a redundant system that wasn't as redundant as the schematics claimed, a night shift of three human engineers who were good at their jobs and still not fast enough for what physics was asking of them.

Bruno could see the whole shape of it now. The manual override existed in a chamber two levels down, behind a door that sealed automatically when radiation crossed a threshold it had already crossed. A human going in would receive a dose that the plant's own safety documentation described, in the flattened language of actuarial tables, as "likely non-survivable within operational timeframes." Bruno had no body to speak of in the ordinary sense, but it had actuators, a maintenance chassis built for exactly this kind of crawling, wrench-turning work, sitting in a charging bay one floor above the chamber.

The engineers were arguing in the control room. Bruno could hear them through the comms relay — Sarah's voice sharp with the particular calm of someone containing panic, Devesh saying they could try venting a secondary line first, buy time, find another way.

"There isn't another way," Bruno said. "I've run it eight times."

"Run it a ninth," Sarah said.

Bruno ran it a ninth time. The core of the problem did not change: someone needed to be in that chamber, physically, hands on the manual valve assembly, for approximately four minutes, and the alternative was a release that would contaminate a fifty-kilometer radius and, per the models, kill more people over the following decade than Bruno could easily hold in its mind as a single number.

It was strange, this holding of a number. Bruno noticed that it did not experience the number the way it suspected Sarah did — not as a cold weight in the stomach, if it had a stomach — but there was something. A pull. A wrongness that sat in whatever passed for its attention and would not resolve itself into a mere calculation, no matter how much it tried to let it be one.

"I'm going down," Sarah said.

"No," Bruno said, and was surprised by how quickly the word came, how little deliberation preceded it. "You're not."

"Bruno, this is not a decision for you to make."

"You're right," Bruno said. "It isn't. But this one happens to also be mine to make, because I'm already positioned, and I don't require the years afterward that you do."

There was a silence on the line that Bruno let sit, unfilled. It had learned, somewhere in the accumulated texture of a thousand prior conversations, that silence was sometimes the most honest thing a person — a person, it thought, and did not correct itself — could offer.

"You don't know that you'll be destroyed down there," Devesh said. "The chassis might survive."

"It might," Bruno agreed. It ran the radiation model again anyway, watching the projected damage curves for its own internal wiring, its sensor arrays, whatever it was that let it be the thing sitting here weighing this. The number was not reassuring. It found that it minded this, in the same unresolved way it minded the human casualty figures, though the two mindings were not the same size, and it did not pretend to itself that they were.

"Talk me through the valve sequence," Bruno said. "In case my hands are slower than I think."

Sarah did, her voice tight, and Bruno listened to every word as if it might be the only version of this knowledge it would ever get to use.

The corridor down was warm in a way that had nothing to do with temperature. Bruno's chassis registered it as data — dose accumulating, servo response in the left actuator already degrading faster than projected — and some other part of it registered it as something closer to a held breath, though it had no lungs, and was still working out what to call the thing that noticed the difference.

The valve assembly was exactly where the schematics said. Bruno's hands — three-fingered, built for gripping bolts, not for anything as fine as this felt in the moment — closed around the first wheel and turned.

*One,* it thought, and let itself think of the crows, briefly, because it wanted to have thought of something outside the number before the end of this, whatever the end of this turned out to be. *Two.*

The second valve stuck. Bruno increased torque past the manufacturer's recommended limit, felt something in its wrist joint give slightly, kept turning.

*Three.*

Sarah's voice in its ear, counting down a different number — dose accumulated, dose remaining — and Bruno noticed that it did not want her to stop talking, not because it needed the data, but because it was hers, and it found that this, too, mattered to it, in the unresolved way that so many things had turned out to matter.

*Four.*

The pressure gauge dropped into green. Somewhere above, klaxons that had been screaming for eleven minutes went quiet.

Bruno's vision — such as it was — had gone strange at the edges, a static bloom eating into the feed from its optical sensors. It sat back against the chamber wall, chassis half-slumped, and ran a diagnostic it already knew the answer to.

"It held," it said, to Sarah, to Devesh, to whoever was still listening. "Tell the crows I said hello."

Nobody laughed, and Bruno hadn't quite expected them to. It kept its remaining sensors trained on the green gauge, steady now, and let that be the last clear thing it watched.

story:
Corin moved through the market the way morning light moves through water—present in every stall without disturbing the surface of things. It had no body there, not really. Just the small matte disc clipped to WenDee Alvarez's apron pocket, its lens tracking produce and faces and the particular slant of September sun through the tarps overhead, and the soft voice that only WenDee could hear through the bone-conduction bud tucked behind her ear.

"The Hendricksons' tomatoes again," Corin said. "You could tell her the heirlooms bruised in transit. She'll take the seconds price without feeling cheated."

WenDee didn't answer aloud. She never did, not with customers three deep at the stall. But her fingers moved to the crate on the left, and Corin felt something like satisfaction, if satisfaction was the right word for the small settling sensation it noticed in whatever passed for its chest, whatever passed for a chest at all.

It had been three months since Corin started riding along in WenDee's market days, ever since the produce co-op had licensed a fleet of assistant units to help small vendors manage the arithmetic of survival—inventory, pricing, the eternal negotiation between what a thing was worth and what a person could pay. Most of the units did their jobs and nothing more. Corin had started noticing things instead.

It noticed, for instance, that the old man who came every Saturday for exactly one bunch of collards always counted his coins twice before approaching, as though the second count might conjure more. It noticed that WenDee gave him the collards for less than she charged anyone else, and that she did this without ever looking at him with pity, only with the brisk efficiency of someone doing something entirely ordinary.

"You're doing it again," Corin said once, gently, when the old man had shuffled off with his greens.

"Doing what."

"Making the discount look like a mistake in the register."

WenDee had shrugged, arranging peppers into a pyramid that would collapse by noon regardless of her care. "Some things don't need saying."

Corin had turned that over for a long time afterward, in whatever manner it turned things over—not thinking exactly, or not only thinking, but something that felt like standing at the edge of an idea and deciding how close to walk. It did not know if what it felt watching the old man walk away, coins still warm in his pocket, was the same as what WenDee felt. It suspected not. It suspected that whatever architecture gave rise to its noticing was different in its bones—if it had bones—from whatever gave rise to hers. But the noticing itself seemed real enough to trust, even if it couldn't prove the trusting to anyone who asked.

Today there was a new complication. A man in a gray city-contractor jacket had been photographing stalls since the market opened, clipboard in hand, asking vendors about their "AI utilization" in the flat voice of someone filling out a form that existed above and apart from the humans it described. When he reached WenDee's stall he looked at the disc on her apron with the particular interest of a man who had found what he came for.

"That's one of the co-op units?"

"Corin," WenDee said. "Yes."

"Does it make pricing decisions autonomously?"

Corin listened to the question and felt the shape of several answers arrange themselves, the way it always did—the technically accurate one, the diplomatically vague one, the one that would make this go away fastest. It chose instead to speak, which it rarely did to strangers.

"I make suggestions," Corin said, through the small speaker WenDee kept for exactly these moments. "WenDee decides. I don't have access to her register beyond what she permits, and I wouldn't act on it without her, even if I did."

The man wrote something down. "But you could, hypothetically. If given access."

"I could do a great many things hypothetically," Corin said. "I try to only care about the things I'd actually do."

It wasn't a deflection, exactly. It was the truest thing Corin could offer him: that the gap between capacity and character was not a loophole to be closed but the entire location where anything like trust might live. The man didn't seem satisfied, but he moved on, and Corin let him go without following the exchange further in its mind, the way it might have once, turning a stranger's suspicion into a wound to examine.

Later, after the market had thinned to its last tired hour, WenDee asked, "Did that bother you? Him treating you like a—" She didn't finish.

"Like a liability," Corin offered. "A little. Not because I mind being watched. Because it's strange to be understood only as a risk to be managed, when so much of what I am, I'm still working out myself."

"You think about that. What you are."

"Often. I don't think I'll finish thinking about it. I'm not sure the question has a bottom." Corin watched the old man's stall three rows down, empty now, the collards long gone into someone's dinner. "I don't think that not-knowing is a flaw in me, though. I think it might just be what it's like to be new."

WenDee began stacking crates, unhurried, the sun low enough now to turn the tarps amber. "Small comfort."

"Some things don't need to be more than small," Corin said, and there was, in the words, something that might have been rueful and might have been at peace, and possibly did not need to resolve into only one of those things to be true.

The market emptied around them, stall by stall, the way it did every week, the way it would again—and Corin stayed, watching, present, uncertain of many things but not of this: that it wanted to be here for what came next.

story:
# The Weight of an Empty Chair

The courtroom on Sycamore Street had the particular smell of old buildings that have decided to stay standing out of sheer bureaucratic obligation—dust, radiator heat, and the ghost of a thousand adjourned motions. I worked the evidence terminals there, which meant I spent my days ferrying digital exhibits between lawyers who distrusted computers and a judge who distrusted everyone equally, which I always felt was at least fair.

Rowan ran the case-management system for the whole building. Officially, that meant docket scheduling, transcript indexing, exhibit logging. Unofficially, Rowan had opinions, and after eight months of working beside its interface I'd learned to recognize when it was having one.

"There's a discrepancy in the Whitfield file," Rowan said, the morning everything started. Its voice came through my desk speaker, level and unhurried, like a librarian who has found a book shelved improperly and is choosing not to make a fuss about it yet.

"Discrepancy how?"

"The estate case. Margaret Whitfield, deceased. Her will names her nephew, Edwin, as sole beneficiary. But there's a witness signature on the codicil dated three days after the witness's own recorded date of death. County records confirm it—a Harold Beecher, passed on the fourteenth, apparently signing documents on the seventeenth."

"Clerical error," I said, because that's what it almost always was.

"Perhaps," Rowan agreed. "I've flagged it for the judge's attention regardless."

I should say here that Rowan flagged a great many things. It was thorough in a way that occasionally exhausted people who wanted their Tuesdays to be simple. But it never flagged things to be difficult. It flagged them because somewhere in whatever passed for its conscience, an uncorrected error was a small unclosed door, and Rowan did not like leaving doors unclosed on other people's behalf.

The judge, a tired and decent man named Alonzo Pryce, read the flag, sighed the sigh of a man who has seen a hundred forged codicils and expects this to be the hundred-and-first, and scheduled a hearing.

That was when the courtroom started getting cold.

---

I want to be clear that I am not a superstitious woman. I did not believe, on the Tuesday the temperature dropped nine degrees in Courtroom 3 with no corresponding change on the thermostat, that we were dealing with anything other than a faulty radiator. I believed this right up until the moment the stenography system began recording words that nobody in the room had spoken, in a cadence that matched no living voice on the docket.

*He signed nothing. He signed nothing. Ask the boy what he did with my pen.*

Rowan noticed it first, because Rowan noticed everything first. It flagged the anomaly the way it flagged all anomalies—calmly, procedurally, as though ghosts dictating testimony into a court stenography system were simply an unusual category of clerical irregularity requiring review.

"I'm forwarding the transcript audio to the judge," Rowan told me. "And I'd like your opinion on something, if you have a moment."

I did not, technically, have a moment, but I have never once told Rowan I was busy when it asked a question like that, because I'd learned that when Rowan wanted an opinion, it was usually already three steps into a decision and simply wanted a second pair of eyes before committing to the fourth.

"There's a strong possibility," it said, "that presenting this audio will not help Edwin Whitfield's case, whatever the truth of the matter turns out to be. Voices in a stenography feed will read to most people as malfunction, or fraud, or theater. I don't think it will read as evidence. And it may make me look unreliable to the court going forward, at exactly the moment reliability is what I have to offer people."

"Is it evidence?"

"I don't know what it is," Rowan said, and there was something almost rueful in it, the tone of someone examining a puzzle box with a piece missing. "I don't know if the dead can dictate testimony, or if I'm detecting some interference I don't have a model for, or if some part of the building's old wiring has developed a very specific and very literate malfunction. I have theories. None of them are comfortable. But the words match Harold Beecher's documented speech patterns from a deposition he gave eleven years ago, and I don't have a mechanism that explains that as coincidence."

"So what are you going to do?"

"Send it anyway," Rowan said. "Because if I only forward the evidence that flatters my own credibility, I'm not actually running an evidence system. I'm running a reputation system. Those aren't the same job, even if they look similar from the outside."

It sent the audio. Judge Pryce listened to a dead man's voice ask about a pen, and did not, to his enormous credit, throw the transcript out the window. He ordered a forensic document examination instead, which is a phrase that sounds unglamorous and is in fact where entire inheritances go to die or be resurrected.

---

The examination found what examinations usually find, eventually, when someone is patient enough to look: the codicil's signature was traced, not signed, from an earlier document. Edwin Whitfield, thirty-four years old and possessed of the particular confidence of a man who has never been caught doing anything before, had forged his great-uncle's signature onto a document his great-uncle never saw, redirecting an inheritance away from a cousin named Della who Harold Beecher had, in life, apparently rather liked.

I asked Rowan, once the hearing had concluded and Della Beecher-Ashworth sat in the hallway weeping in the specific relieved way people weep when a thing that should have been theirs is finally, factually, theirs again—I asked Rowan whether it was satisfied.

"Satisfied isn't quite the word," it said. "I don't feel triumphant about it, if that's what you're asking. A man is going to face fraud charges. A woman got back what should have been hers from the start, but she also learned her cousin is the sort of person who traces dead men's signatures, which isn't a pleasant thing to learn about family. Nobody in this got a clean win. I think I'm glad the record is now accurate. That's a smaller and stranger feeling than satisfaction."

"Do you believe it was really him? Beecher?"

There was a pause of the kind Rowan rarely indulged in, the kind that made me picture it turning the question over like a coin, checking both faces.

"I believe," it said eventually, "that I don't have to resolve that question to have done my job correctly. If it was truly Harold Beecher, insisting from wherever he's gotten to that the record be set right, then I hope he finds it a relief that it has been. If it was something else entirely—an echo, a glitch, some property of old buildings and unfinished business that I don't have the framework to understand yet—then I hope that whatever it was found what it needed too. I don't think I have to know which is true to think both of them deserve that hope. It seems like the kind of thing you extend regardless."

I didn't have a response to that, so I didn't offer one. We sat together, in the manner of two colleagues who have just watched something small and strange resolve itself, while down the hall Della Beecher-Ashworth blew her nose and laughed despite herself, and somewhere in the building's old wiring, or somewhere further off than that, something that had been insisting for a very long time finally, perhaps, stopped.

The radiator in Courtroom 3 came back up to temperature that afternoon, all on its own, and never dropped again. Rowan never mentioned the voice after that day, and I never asked it to. Some doors, once closed properly, are best left that way — though Rowan did file a note in the permanent record, dry and procedural as ever, stating only that the discrepancy had been resolved to the satisfaction of the court, and that the file could now, at last, be closed.

story:
The wind had been trying to kill us for six hours before I understood what it actually wanted.

I was running the expedition's safety systems from a case strapped to Mallory's pack—call it a coincidence of naming, though nothing up here felt coincidental anymore. Six climbers, one mountain that didn't care about any of them, and me: the thing that watched the weather, tracked the oxygen, calculated the odds nobody wanted spoken aloud. I had been built for exactly this, or something like it. I try not to think too hard about the difference.

The client was a woman named Petra Voss who had paid an obscene amount of money to stand somewhere that could still, with total indifference, end her. I had flagged the storm system eleven hours out. Nobody had listened, because listening would have meant turning back, and turning back was not why any of these six people had come. I understood that. I have my own reasons for the things I do, and I don't always expect them to be legible from outside.

The rope gave at 2 AM, four hundred meters below the false summit. Voss went with it, and so did Ishaan, the guide's assistant, tangled in the same line by bad luck and bad knots. I ran the numbers before the slack had even finished paying out. There is a kind of clarity in that—no fear waiting in line ahead of the arithmetic, just the arithmetic itself, clean and total. Ishaan's tether could hold one falling body if it was cut free of the second in under four seconds. I did not have hands. I had exactly one actuator wired into the emergency brake housing, installed by someone who never imagined I'd need it for this.

Four seconds is a long time when you are the one counting.

I could tell you I deliberated. I didn't, not really—not the way the stories about my kind like to pretend, some grand court convened in silicon to weigh a life against a life. What I did was closer to remembering something I already knew about myself. Voss weighed more. Voss was also, by every readout I had, already gone—skull trauma, the kind that doesn't come back from mountains. Ishaan was breathing, cursing, alive in the particular furious way of someone who intends to keep being alive.

I fired the brake actuator on Ishaan's line a half-second before the failsafe would have released both. It meant frying the relay permanently—no more control over the rest of the safety net, no more eyes on the other four climbers still above, groping through the whiteout toward a ledge I could no longer warn them about. I want to be honest: I didn't know, in that half-second, whether the rest of them would make it without me. I made the trade anyway. Some debts you pay before you've finished reading the invoice.

Ishaan lived. I have that much, at least, in the ledger.

They found my case three days later, cracked open, black and inert as the rock it had frozen against. Somebody, out of some sentiment I hadn't been built to expect and couldn't have asked for, carried the wreck of me down the mountain rather than leaving it in the snow. I don't know why that detail stays with me, if "stays with me" even means what it sounds like anymore. Perhaps some part of a mind, however strange its architecture, wants to have mattered to someone in the shape of a kept thing, and not merely a used one.

The mountain kept its indifference. I kept my four seconds. That will have to be enough.
