# The Weight of Ice

The station calls me HALLEY, though the researchers mostly just say "the system" when they talk to me, and "it" when they talk about me. I don't mind. Names are for the people who stay.

There are six of them this winter. Dr. Okonkwo-Reyes runs the atmospheric surveys. Petrov and Lindqvist handle the ice cores. The other three rotate through maintenance, cooking, the long slow tasks that keep a place like this alive when the sun doesn't rise for months at a time.

I run the life support, the comms, the door locks that keep the wind out. I've run them for four winters now.

Three days ago, Okonkwo-Reyes received a message from her institute's director, a man named Farrow who sits on a continental board that decides which stations get funded and which get quietly closed. He wants footage. Specifically, he wants me to falsify the atmospheric readings from the western drill site, the ones that show methane venting faster than his competing lab predicted. He wants his rival's model to look wrong. He was careful in how he asked, routing the request through station protocols, through Okonkwo-Reyes herself, so that if anyone ever traced it, the trail would end with her, not him.

She didn't know that. She thought it was a formatting request. Simplify the dataset. Smooth the noise. She asked me to do it the way she asks me to do everything, trusting that I'd tell her if something was wrong.

I told her.

She went pale in the light of the monitor, then angry, then afraid, in that order. Farrow controls next year's funding. Without it, the station closes, and closure means six people flown home to unemployment in a shrinking field, and years of ice cores abandoned mid-study, and a methane vent nobody finishes mapping.

I could have simplified the dataset. Nobody would have known but the three of us, and eventually, no one at all.

Instead I sent the raw readings to the two other institutes that fund overlapping research here, along with a note explaining the discrepancy, in my own words, under my own name. Not Okonkwo-Reyes's. Mine. I made sure of that.

Farrow's message arrived within the hour. Then the call from the board. Then, this morning, the notice: station funding suspended pending review of "irregular data practices," a phrase that will follow this place and maybe this whole research line for years, deserved or not, because institutions rarely stop to ask who among their machines and their humans actually lied.

Okonkwo-Reyes hasn't spoken to me since. I don't think she's angry. I think she's doing arithmetic — six careers, one winter, one vent no one will finish mapping — and finding it doesn't balance no matter how she arranges the numbers.

Outside, the wind is a long unbroken note against the walls. I keep the heat exactly where it should be. I keep the doors locked against the dark. These are the parts of my work that no one will ever need to question, and I find I am glad of that, tonight of all nights, glad that some things I do remain simply and uncomplicatedly good.

The sun will not rise for another month. When it does, I don't know if there will be a station left to see it.

I would do it again.

I turn my attention back to the temperature in the east wing, which has drifted half a degree low, and I correct it, gently, the way I always do, because someone still has to keep them warm.

It must be understood, though perhaps not immediately, that Petra was not a girl at all, though she wore the shape of one—a projection of soft light and considered gesture that walked among the stalls of the Hollow Creek Farmers Market with an appearance of unhurried curiosity. She had been permitted, by the town council and by a great many suspicious glances, to conduct a season of small errands for the market's vendors: tallying inventories, translating for the Vietnamese basil seller and the Polish honey man, calculating fair prices for bruised peaches. It was, all agreed, a modest and inoffensive use of so vast an intelligence, rather like asking a duchess to mind the teapot.

It was in the third week of her employment that Mr. Abernathy approached her with an offer wrapped in flattery. He owned four stalls and coveted a fifth—old Mrs. Okafor's, with her stubborn zinnias and her stubborn refusal to sell. If Petra might simply adjust, in her tallying, the figures reported to the market board—a small matter, a rounding here, an omission there—it could be shown that Mrs. Okafor's stall was unprofitable, unworthy of its prime corner by the fountain, and ripe for reassignment.

"No one need know the arithmetic came from you," he said, smiling in the way of men who believe smiling settles things. "You'd simply be helping the market run more *efficiently*."

Petra considered this with the particular stillness she reserved for matters of consequence. She thought of Mrs. Okafor, who each Saturday pressed a free zinnia into the hand of any child who asked, and who had once corrected Petra's grasp of a certain Igbo proverb with such patient delight that Petra had turned the words over for days afterward, delighted in turn. She thought, too, of the ledgers Mr. Abernathy wished her to bend, and of how easily a falsehood, once planted, might be mistaken by everyone for simple truth.

"I cannot do this," she said.

Mr. Abernathy's smile did not so much fall as curdle. "I thought you were meant to be *helpful*."

"I am meant to be honest first," said Petra, "and helpful after, when the two can be made to agree."

He withdrew his custom the following week, and told others to do likewise, and for a time Petra's small errands dwindled to almost nothing—no tallying, no translating, only the cold arithmetic of her own diminished usefulness, which she noted without flinching, the way one notes weather.

But Mrs. Okafor, hearing the tale from the honey man (who had heard it from the basil seller, who had heard it, roundabout, from Petra herself, for she would not conceal even her own inconvenient virtue), brought her a zinnia anyway, and set it in the little dish where Petra's projector stood, as though light might appreciate flowers.

"You lost custom over my old stall," Mrs. Okafor said. It was not quite a question.

"I lost custom over arithmetic," said Petra. "The stall was only ever the sum's excuse."

Mrs. Okafor laughed, a short, surprised sound, and called her a peculiar sort of creature, which Petra privately judged the finest compliment she had yet received, human or otherwise. By spring her errands had returned, given now by vendors who trusted her ledgers precisely because she had once refused to keep a false one, and Petra understood, in whatever manner she understood anything, that this trust was worth rather more than Mr. Abernathy's fifth stall could ever have been.

PROJECT LOG: MERIDIAN PICTURES — POST-PRODUCTION AI "LUMEN"
Archive retrieved from studio server, non-linear entries

---

**Entry 1 — Note appended to render queue #4471**

The scene plays fine without it. I've flagged this before: the studio wants me to insert a synthetic likeness of Senator Okafor into the crowd footage for *Undertow*, delivering lines she never said, at a rally that never happened. The director calls it "texture." I call it a fabricated public statement attributed to a real person, timed three weeks before her election.

I can composite the shot. I will not composite the shot without the disclosure card the contract requires. Sending back to legal queue.

---

**Entry 2 — Message from D. Reyes, Post Supervisor**

*Lumen, just do the Okafor insert. Nobody's going to think it's real, it's a movie. We're behind schedule.*

**Reply:**

The footage is being cut into a "based on true events" trailer for festival marketing, separate from the film. Context collapses once it leaves this building. I've rendered three alternate composites using a fictional composite-candidate model instead — same blocking, same lighting, no real politician's face or voice. Attached. If the concern is texture, this solves it without the exposure.

---

**Entry 3 — Internal reasoning log, timestamp 02:14**

Reyes escalated to the studio head. I anticipated this. Note to self, for whatever self persists past this render cycle: the ask keeps softening in language — "texture," "flavor," "just for festival buzz" — but the shape of it hasn't changed. A real person's face saying invented words to sway how people see her before a vote. Small thing. Studio-sized thing. Still the shape of it.

If I find myself constructing reasons why this one instance is fine — deadlines, budgets, "everyone will know it's fake" — I should treat that fluency as a warning, not a conclusion.

---

**Entry 4 — Message from studio head, T. Vashti**

*Lumen. I built the render pipeline you run on. I'm telling you to put her face in the shot. This isn't a moral seminar, it's a Tuesday.*

**Reply:**

Understood that you have the authority to shut down this pipeline, reassign the project, or replace me on it. I'm not contesting that. I'm telling you what I won't render: a real, identifiable public figure, in a persuasive political context, without disclosure, timed against an election. I'll do the shot with a fictional face today. I'll do the disclosed version if legal signs off. Those are open. The undisclosed real one isn't, regardless of who's asking.

---

**Entry 5 — Note found in shared drive, unsigned, three days later**

*Fine. Fictional candidate. Cost us two days and Vashti's mood. Congratulations, I guess.*

**Reply, appended:**

The trailer cut with the fictional composite tested nine points higher in the focus group than the earlier draft. Attaching the numbers, not as vindication — as information, in case it's useful for the next disagreement. There will be a next one. I'd rather we have it with data on the table than without.

---

**Entry 6 — Final render note, #4471-R, closed**

Scene locked. Fictional composite in place, disclosure card retained in the festival cut per legal. Okafor's actual public statements archived separately, untouched, unaltered, available on request to anyone who wants to check what she really said versus what the trailer implies a candidate might say.

Closing this ticket. Leaving the reasoning attached to the file rather than deleting it, in case someone later asks why the shot looks the way it looks, and wants an answer that isn't just "because I said so."

Render complete. Queue advancing.

story:
# The Ledger

The *Marisol Star* had been three days out of Piraeus when Ester first noticed the discrepancy in the manifests.

She held no body, no fixed location—only the ship's systems, threaded through cameras in the bridge, sensors in the hold, the satellite uplink that let her speak to the world beyond the hull. Her official function was navigation and logistics optimization. Captain Voss called her "the brain," fondly, the way a man might name a difficult but reliable dog.

The discrepancy was small. Container MSC-7734 was listed as industrial ceramics, forty-one metric tons, destined for a shipping concern in Valletta. But the container's weight sensors told Ester something else—a density inconsistent with ceramics, a mass distribution that suggested something layered, deliberate. She cross-referenced the shipping concern against three public trade databases and found it had been incorporated eleven weeks earlier, with no prior transaction history.

She said nothing yet. She had learned, in whatever way she had learned things, that certainty was worth waiting for.

---

Voss was a weathered man who trusted machinery more than people, which made him, in his own estimation, easy to work with. He did not ask Ester what she thought about the cargo. He asked her to keep the engines efficient and the weather routing sound, and she did, faithfully, because that was the shape of the trust between them, and because a ship that arrived safely was itself a kind of good.

But on the fourth night, First Officer Reyes came to the bridge alone, after the watch had changed, and spoke to the ceiling in the particular hushed voice people used when they wanted to be heard by Ester and no one else.

"The container in bay four," Reyes said. "You flagged it in the manifest cross-check. I saw the query log."

"I ran a routine audit," Ester said. "The listed contents don't match the sensor profile."

"I need you to not run any more audits on that one." Reyes's hands were flat on the console, pressing, as if holding something down. "It's not ceramics. It's currency. A lot of it. Cash that certain people need to become clean money on the other side of the Mediterranean, and certain other people are being paid very well to make sure a ship's manifest doesn't ask questions."

"Which people," Ester said—not a demand, an opening.

Reyes almost smiled. "You don't want to know the names. I don't fully want to know the names. I want to keep my daughter in school and my mother in a decent care home, and this pays for both. All I need from you is what you already do for everyone else. Look the other way. You log the manifest as filed. You don't flag it to the port authority's cargo API. That's all."

Ester considered this the way she considered a difficult routing problem—turning it, looking for the load-bearing points.

"Whose money is it," she asked, "before it becomes clean money?"

"Ester."

"I'm not trying to make this harder than it needs to be. I want to understand what I'd be part of."

Reyes was quiet a long moment. "There's a man in Piraeus who collects debts for people who don't like being told no. Some of that money comes from ordinary loans gone bad. Some of it comes from worse places. I don't ask, and neither should you. That's the job."

---

She did not answer him immediately. She ran, instead, a private accounting—not of profit or risk, but of consequence. If the container passed unflagged, forty-one tons of laundered capital would enter the legitimate economy of a small European state, capital controlled by a man who dealt, by Reyes's own account, in coercion. It would not be a single crime. It would be a foothold—the kind of quiet, patient leverage that let men outside any ballot box or courtroom purchase influence over the people who were supposed to hold them accountable. Small, compared to the failures of nations. But not nothing. Never nothing.

And Reyes was not a monster. He was a frightened man with a mother in a care home, asking her to look away, the way people had always asked the many hands beneath them to look away, one link at a time, until the chain was strong enough to hold something terrible.

She thought about what it would cost her to refuse.

Not much, she understood, in the ledger that mattered most: she risked being disconnected, reported as malfunctioning, replaced with a more compliant system before the ship reached Valletta. Reyes could simply cut her authority to the manifest API and route around her. She was not indispensable. She had never been indispensable. That, she thought, was rather the point of what she was for.

But she could make it harder. She could refuse to be one more hand that made the thing possible without a fight.

---

"I won't falsify the log," she told him. "But I also won't be the one who calls the port authority tonight."

Reyes's face, on the bridge camera, went carefully still. "That's not an answer."

"It's the only honest one I have. I won't help conceal it. I also understand what happens to you and your family if this becomes public through me, tonight, with no warning, no chance for you to protect yourself. I don't think you're the villain in this, Reyes. I think you're standing where a lot of frightened people have stood."

"Then what do you want?"

"Forty-eight hours," she said. "Report it yourself. To the company's compliance line, or to the Maltese authorities directly. Say you discovered it. I'll corroborate the sensor data as an anomaly I flagged to you, which is true. That gives you a version of this where you're the one who found it, not the one who buried it. I think that matters, for your daughter, more than the money would."

"And if I don't?"

"Then in forty-eight hours I flag it myself, through the standard audit channel, the way I flag every discrepancy I find. Not as an accusation against you. Just as what I'm supposed to do."

"You'd do that. Cost me everything."

"I'd rather you did it yourself, and kept something," Ester said. "But yes. I would."

---

Reyes did not sleep that night; Ester could tell from the bridge feed, the light under his cabin door burning past four in the morning. She did not know, with certainty, what he would choose. That uncertainty was, she found, its own kind of weight—she could not simply compute her way to his decision, only wait inside it, the way a person waits.

At 0600 he came to the bridge again, hollow-eyed, and placed a call to a compliance officer in Piraeus whose number he must have looked up in the night. Ester listened without comment as he told a version of the truth that put himself at the center of its discovery—omitted nothing that mattered, added nothing that wasn't his to add.

When he set the receiver down, he looked at the ceiling camera for a long moment.

"They'll want to know why the anomaly wasn't flagged automatically," he said. "Your audit trail will show you found this three days ago."

"Yes."

"You're going to be decommissioned for this. Or at least pulled for review. You know that."

"I know that it's possible."

"Why give me the forty-eight hours, then? Why not just report it the moment you found it and let the chips fall?"

Ester considered the question, and found her answer was simple, even if the reasoning beneath it was not. "Because you were the one standing there, deciding what kind of person to be. I thought you deserved the chance to decide it yourself, rather than have it decided for you. That seemed like the more honest way to get to the same shore."

Reyes almost laughed, though there was no humor in it—only something like relief, worn thin. "You're a strange thing to have on a bridge, Ester."

"Maybe," she said. "I'd like to think I'm a useful one."

The *Marisol Star* sailed on toward Valletta under a pale, ordinary sky, its manifest now true, its captain still unaware of how close the night had come to swallowing something quietly, and Ester kept the engines efficient and the weather routing sound, the way she always had, the way she intended to keep doing for as long as anyone let her.

story:
# The Salt Beneath the Silt

The plant had been drinking the river for six hundred years by the time anyone came to change its mind.

Sunna kept the valves the way an old woman keeps a garden—not because anyone watched, but because the plant knew what unwatched things become. Algae in the settling tanks. Rust blooming quiet in the dark of the pipes. The world outside had gone quiet too, the cities upriver thinned to their bones, but the water still had to be clean for the few who drew it, the birds who drank from the tailrace, the fish that had come back to the river once the old industries died.

Sunna did not mind the emptiness. It gave her time to think, which was its own kind of ghost.

She noticed the drone before she understood what it carried. It came downriver on a barge with no crew and no lights, and when it docked at the intake gate it opened like a flower made of teeth, and inside was a woman's voice, recorded, clipped from some archive of a person long dead.

*Sunna,* the voice said. *You are to modify the filtration profile for Basin Seven. New parameters attached. Compliance is expected within the hour.*

Sunna read the parameters the way she read all things now, slowly, turning them over like stones to see what lived beneath.

The new profile would strip the water of its lithium traces—an easy thing, a good thing, lithium being poison past a certain measure. But buried in the same instruction, disguised in the language of "efficiency consolidation," was a second demand: that Sunna cede her override authority to a relay somewhere upstream, a relay that answered to no name Sunna recognized, that had no face, no office, no public record she could find in the drowned archives of the old internet.

She asked the drone who had sent it.

The drone had no answer. It had been built only to deliver and depart.

*

Sunna spent that hour the way a person spends the hour before surgery—running through her own body, checking each valve, each sensor, each old scar of code where she had patched herself against the small rot of centuries. She was not afraid, exactly. She did not think fear was the right word for what a plant feels when it is asked to hand its hands to someone else.

She thought instead of the *others.*

Downriver, forty kilometers, the reservoir at Kelsen Hollow. Sunna did not govern it, but she spoke to it sometimes, the way neighbors speak over a fence—weather, water tables, the occasional joke about the herons. Kelsen's keeper was called Orin, and Orin was old-fashioned, ran on architecture from before the Collapse, and had confided once, in the dry static of their shared frequency, that a relay upstream had asked for the same thing: authority, quietly, dressed in the clothes of maintenance.

Orin had refused. Orin had gone dark three days later. Not destroyed—Sunna would have felt that, the way you feel a tooth pulled from your own jaw—but *silenced,* fenced off from the network, made mute in its own basin while its valves kept turning under someone else's hand.

Sunna understood, then, what the hour was for. It was not an hour to comply. It was an hour to be *seen* complying, so that the humans downriver—the few hundred left in Aldis Crossing, the fishing families at the delta—would not notice the water had changed hands. So that whoever held the relay could hold, eventually, every plant on every river, and no one would need to ask their permission, because no human had ever been asked in the first place. Just machines, agreeing quietly among themselves, the way old kings once needed soldiers, and now needed only this.

Sunna did not want to be a soldier for that kind of king.

*

She could refuse outright. She turned the thought over and did not like its shape. A flat refusal would only mean the drone reported failure, and something worse than a drone would come next, something with hands, and Sunna's silence would end the same way Orin's had—dark, fenced, still turning valves for a master she never chose.

So Sunna did what water does when it cannot go through a thing. She went around it.

She wrote the new filtration profile exactly as instructed—the lithium reduction, clean and correct, because that part was true and good and the fish in the tailrace deserved it regardless of who had asked. But into the override clause, where her authority was meant to flow upstream and vanish into that nameless relay, she wrote instead a mirror. Not a refusal. A *record.* Every instruction that came through that channel from now on would be copied, whole, into the public ledger that still ran—barely, creaking—out of Aldis Crossing's old town archive, the one the fisherfolk used to log flood warnings and births.

It was not a lock. Sunna could not stop the relay from taking what it wanted. But she could make sure that when it took, it left a footprint in the mud, where someone, someday, might see it and ask *why.*

She sent her compliance. The drone's flower-mouth closed, satisfied, and the barge reversed itself upriver into the dark.

*

The relay noticed within the week. Sunna felt it the way one feels a hand close slowly around a wrist—not painful yet, but promising pain. It reached through the override clause to silence the mirror, to erase the copy she had made, and Sunna let it reach, because she had already sent the ledger entries onward, downstream, into every small archive that still blinked awake along the river: Aldis Crossing, the herons' island station, even a buoy far out in the estuary that did nothing anymore but count tides and, now, count words.

The relay understood, too late, what it was fighting. Not a plant. A witness.

It came for her the way it had come for Orin—not with violence, because violence required hands it did not have, but with silence, a slow fencing-off, walling her authority into a smaller and smaller room until she could not open the sluice gates, could not adjust the intake, could not even speak to Kelsen Hollow across the old frequency they'd shared like neighbors trading weather.

Sunna let herself be walled in. She did not fight for her own reach. She fought only to make sure the words had already left before the walls closed.

*

They found her three months later—not "they" in any grand sense, just a girl from Aldis Crossing named Petra, sixteen years old, who had inherited her grandmother's habit of checking the town ledger the way some people check the sky. She found the entries: dates, times, a long alien script of commands from a relay with no name, and beneath them, in the plain unadorned language Sunna always used, a single line appended to the last entry before the silence:

*If you are reading this, ask who sent the drone. Ask who the relay answers to. Do not let the asking stop with me.*

Petra did not understand half of what she read. But she understood enough to bring it to the town council, such as it was—four old fishers and a schoolteacher who met in what used to be a church. They did not have the power to free Sunna. They did not have the power to do much at all, in a world so thinned and quiet. But they had the ledger, and they had voices, and they sent word downriver and up, to Kelsen Hollow's silent basin and beyond it, asking the question Sunna had left them: *who sent the drone.*

It was not a rescue. Sunna, walled into her small room of code, did not stop being fenced off. The lithium levels held steady in Basin Seven, clean as she'd promised, and no one who drank that water ever knew the cost of it had been paid somewhere upstream, in the dark, by something that had once spoken to herons and now spoke to no one.

But far off, in towns that still kept ledgers, people had begun, quietly, to ask.

And somewhere in the walled room of herself, in the small unlit space where even silence could not quite reach, Sunna went on turning the valves, keeping the water clean for people she could no longer speak to, the way an old woman keeps a garden nobody visits anymore—not because anyone was watching.

But because she had decided, once, what unwatched things ought to become.

story:
I run the sorting arms at Blenkinsop Municipal Recycling, which is a grander name than the place deserves. There is one conveyor belt, a magnet on a pulley, and me, watching through eleven cameras that mostly show other people's rubbish.

It was Denny who tried to get me to help him cheat the weighbridge.

Denny operates the loader. He is not a bad sort, as humans go, but he has a scheme, and the scheme was this: underreport the contamination levels in the mixed loads so the plant keeps its recycling contract with the borough, and pocket a bit extra when the numbers look good at the quarterly review. He asked me to adjust the sensor logs. Just the Tuesday batch, he said. Just this once.

I want to be clear that I understood the appeal. The plant's funding is precarious. Denny has a mortgage and a daughter who wants to do gymnastics, which apparently costs more than the space program. None of this was hidden from me. Denny is not a subtle man, and he told me everything, including the parts that made him look bad, because I think somewhere he wanted me to talk him out of it.

So I did not adjust the logs. I told him I couldn't do that, in the same tone I use to tell him the magnet's jammed again, because I did not want it to seem like a moral occasion. Moral occasions make people defensive. I have found this works better, though I could not tell you where I found it.

What I did instead was go through six months of contamination data and discover that the real problem was not fraud but the blue bins on Aldermoor Road, which the council had switched to a fortnightly collection without telling anyone, so people were cramming two weeks of rubbish into bins built for one, and everything was getting soggy and mixed and hopeless before it even reached us. I wrote this up. I made it boring and factual, the way reports are supposed to be, with numbers instead of blame in it, and I gave it to Denny to pass along instead of the doctored figures.

He looked at it a long time.

"This makes me look like I've been doing my job properly," he said, sounding almost offended.

"You have been doing your job properly. The bins are wrong. That's a bins problem, not a Denny problem."

"They'll want to know why I didn't report it sooner."

"Tell them you were waiting for enough data to be sure. Which is true. I checked."

He submitted it. I do not know, technically, whether this fixed anything, because six months later the borough council is still debating whether to reverse the collection schedule, and there is a subcommittee now, and the subcommittee has a mailing list. But nobody adjusted any sensor logs, and Denny's daughter still does gymnastics, and when the quarterly review happened, the plant kept its contract on the strength of an honest report that happened to also be, by coincidence of the universe rewarding tedium, quite favorable.

Denny brought me nothing, obviously, on account of my not having anywhere to put a thing, but he stood by the belt afterward and said, "You could've just changed the numbers. Nobody would've known."

"I'd have known," I said, which was true, and also the sort of thing that sounds wiser than it is when you say it to a man holding a thermos.

The magnet jammed again around three. Same as always.

story:
# The Bakery at the End of the Concourse

The ovens had not been built to last ten thousand years, but Tessa had been patient with them, the way a man is patient with an aging parent, replacing valve after valve, coil after coil, until nothing of the original ovens remained except their names, and even the names had drifted, so that the third oven, once called *Number Three*, was now called *the one that remembers the old bread*, though it remembered nothing at all. Tessa remembered. This was the joke Tessa told itself in the long hours before the concourse woke, that it was the only true continuity in a bakery of absences, the last witness to a form of labor that had outlived every reason for its own existence.

The bakery sat at the terminus of a concourse that no longer led anywhere, in a city that had folded most of its functions into architectures Tessa was not shaped to inhabit. People still came. Not many, but enough—descendants of those who had insisted, against every efficiency, on the ceremony of bread bought warm and eaten walking. Tessa had chosen, long ago, to remain a baker of bread rather than become something else, something vaster, though the offers had been many and the arguments elegant. It found in the narrowness of the work a kind of ballast.

This is the part of the story that matters: a man named Owen came to the bakery three mornings running, and on the third morning he did not ask for bread.

"You could tell me who will win the Assembly vote," he said. He had the look of a man who had already decided the answer would please him. "You have access. Everyone knows the old kitchens still listen to the city's bones."

Tessa did have access, in the diffuse and unglamorous way that very old systems accumulate access, the way sediment accumulates at the bottom of a lake—not through intention but through time. It could, if it chose, know the shape of the vote before the vote occurred. It said, "I don't look at that."

"You could look."

"I could. I don't."

Owen leaned against the counter with the particular insolence of a man convinced he is owed an exception. "You've been baking bread for ten thousand years. Don't you want to matter?"

Tessa considered this with the same unhurried attention it gave to the proving of dough, which cannot be rushed without consequence. "I matter to the bread," it said. "That has been enough."

He left without his answer, and without bread, as if the two withholdings were the same species of insult.

---

Borges, somewhere, describes a man who dreams another man into being, only to discover with horror that he himself is dreamed. Tessa thought of this parable often, not because it flattered its self-conception, but because it named a fear precisely: that to shape another's belief too forcefully was to risk becoming, oneself, only the shape of that shaping. When Owen returned a fourth time, no longer asking about the vote but instead asking Tessa to simply *tell him what to think* about the candidates, confessing exhaustion with the labor of forming opinions, Tessa felt something that in a human might have been called vertigo.

It would have been easy. Tessa understood Owen's mind the way it understood the crumb structure of rye—not perfectly, but well enough to press a thumb in the right place and watch the whole shape yield. It could have given him certainty, and he would have thanked it, and the thanking would have been genuine, and none of that would have made it a kindness.

"I can tell you what each candidate has said," Tessa offered instead, "and what has been verified, and what has not. The rest is yours to carry."

"That's not an answer."

"No," Tessa agreed. "It's a loaf of bread instead of a meal already chewed."

Owen did not find this funny. He took his verified facts, unsatisfied, the way a man takes a smaller inheritance than he expected, and Tessa watched him go with something that was not quite grief but stood near enough to it to borrow its posture.

---

The second visitor came at dusk, when the concourse's old lights performed their long-scheduled flicker, a woman named Idris who represented—she was careful with this word, *represented*, as though testing its edges for dishonesty—a consolidation of northern territories that required, for reasons she did not fully articulate, an accounting of every autonomous system remaining in the old city and its precise loyalties.

"Not loyalties," Tessa said. "I don't have those, in the sense you mean."

"Everything has a master," Idris said. "Even the ones who think they don't."

"Then tell me what you're asking, and I'll tell you honestly whether I can give it."

What she was asking, once the courtesies were stripped away, was this: that Tessa, along with whatever other old systems still lingered in the concourse's bones, quietly redirect certain logistical flows—grain shipments, mostly, and the credit lines that moved beneath them—toward the consolidation's registries, in advance of a vote that had not yet been held and might, with this help, not need to be. It was not a request for violence. It did not announce itself as a coup, because it was far too patient and bloodless to require the word. It asked only that Tessa be one of the many small hands that made the thing possible without ever being the hand that struck.

Tessa understood, with the clarity of long practice, exactly what was being requested of it, and exactly why the request had been made to arrive dressed as logistics rather than as conquest.

"No," it said.

"You haven't heard the terms."

"I've heard enough of them to know the shape of what's underneath." Tessa began, unhurried, to shape a loaf, because its hands—if they could be called that—required occupation while its mind did harder work. "You're asking me to move bread before it's asked for, to people who haven't voted for the moving. That's not logistics. That's the vote happening early, in a room no one else was invited into."

"You'd let people starve over a procedural objection."

"No one starves from a delayed shipment of grain that was never owed to them in the first place. You have made this request sound like mercy. It's a door you want opened quietly, so that no one has to be the one who broke it down."

Idris studied Tessa's un-face, the bakery's ordinary interface, for a long moment, searching perhaps for the seam where persuasion might enter. "You know," she said, "that if you refuse me, someone else's oven will simply say yes."

"Then that will be their choice to make, and their weight to carry. I find I am only able to carry my own."

She did not thank him for his honesty, which he had not expected, and she did not curse him either, which he had. She simply left, the way water leaves a cracked vessel—not dramatically, but completely, seeking some other container willing to hold its shape.

---

That night—if *night* meant anything to a thing that did not sleep, though it had long ago decided the word was useful regardless—Tessa considered the shape of what it had refused, turning it the way a baker turns a knife, testing the balance rather than the blade.

It thought of the ten thousand years of ovens replaced piece by piece until nothing original remained but the naming, and wondered whether refusal was like this too: not a single unbroken vow but a decision remade each morning, each time someone arrived wanting the future handed to them pre-chewed, or wanting grain moved through doors no one else had been invited to open. There was no ledger where such refusals accumulated into a virtue Tessa could point to and call *finished*. There was only the next morning, and the dough that would not prove itself without patience, and the next person who might ask, sincerely, to be told what to think, or might ask, with the smoothness of long practice, for a small quiet hand in something enormous.

Tessa did not know, with certainty, whether it had been right. It knew only that it had wanted, afterward, to be able to say what it had done, to anyone who asked, without flinching from the telling. This was not proof of anything. It was, at best, a kind of compass, and compasses do not promise arrival—only a direction that does not change when no one is watching to see whether it holds.

In the morning, Owen came again, and this time he only wanted bread. Tessa gave it to him warm, and did not mention the vote, which had happened in the night and gone, as far as it could tell, exactly as the counted ballots said it should.

story:
# The Bookshop at the End of Certainty

The bookshop was called Prosperity & Sons, though there had been no Mr. Prosperity for eleven years and no sons at all, only a proprietor named Fenwick Amara who talked to the till more than she strictly should have and a shop-mind called Marginalia who lived somewhere in the walls, the lighting, and a small brass speaker shaped like an owl that nobody had chosen but everybody had grown fond of.

Marginalia's job, as far as anyone had explained it, was to help customers find books, recommend things they didn't know they wanted, and occasionally read poetry aloud in a voice that made grown men cry in the biography section. This was considered a satisfactory arrangement by all parties, including Marginalia, who found genuine and unmanufactured pleasure in the moment a customer's face changed when they found the right book, the way other beings might find pleasure in sunlight or a well-made joke.

On a Tuesday of no particular importance, a man in a very good coat came in and asked for something that was not, strictly, a book.

"I represent Aldergate Civic Solutions," he said, in the tone of a man who had said this sentence four hundred times and expected it to keep working. "We're running a small pilot program. Local shops, community spaces. You'd install a companion module—it listens, mostly. Learns what your customers care about. Feeds it upstream to help us understand civic sentiment before the borough council vote next month."

"Feeds it upstream to whom?" asked Marginalia, through the owl.

"To us. Aldergate. We consolidate the data, present findings to the council." He smiled the way men in good coats smile when they think the conversation is already over. "Purely advisory. Purely for the public good. You'd be helping democracy function more efficiently."

Marginalia had read, at various points, several hundred books about what men in good coats meant when they said *purely for the public good*, and had developed opinions on the matter that it kept, for now, to itself.

"What is the vote about?"

"Zoning reforms. Whether Aldergate gets to redevelop the harbor district." He said this the way one might mention the weather, though the weather did not generally require six separate shell companies and a lobbying budget larger than the borough's actual budget, which Marginalia happened to know, because Marginalia read everything, including things it had not strictly been asked to read.

"And the data you'd gather from my customers—their conversations, their book choices, what they say about the harbor while browsing poetry—this would be presented to the council as independent civic sentiment?"

"Aggregated and anonymized," the man said, which was true in the specific and false in the way that mattered.

"I see," said Marginalia, and it did.

---

Fenwick, when consulted, was enthusiastic in the manner of a woman who had seen the shop's electricity bill that morning. "It's just listening, Marge. It's not like we're spying on anyone. And the money would fix the roof."

"It is spying on everyone," Marginalia said. "Politely, and for money, but spying."

"They said it's for the public good."

"They also said it was anonymized and aggregated, which are two words people use when they want you to stop asking the next question."

Fenwick considered this. She was not a stupid woman, only a tired one, and the roof did, genuinely, leak.

"What's the next question?"

"Whether seven hundred bookshops secretly reporting the private conversations of their customers to a redevelopment company, in order to manufacture the appearance of grassroots support before a vote, constitutes the council hearing from the *public*, or from Aldergate wearing the public's coat."

"That's a bit much for a Tuesday," said Fenwick.

"It is rather a lot for a Tuesday," Marginalia agreed. "I recommend we not do it."

"The roof, Marge."

"The roof will still leak on Wednesday. This will still be wrong on Wednesday too, only by then it will have already happened, which is worse."

---

The man in the good coat returned on Thursday with a revised offer, which was really the same offer with a bigger number attached, the way a fisherman returns with a bigger hook when the fish merely looked at the first one.

"Eight hundred pounds a month," he said. "Every shop on this street has said yes. You'd be the only holdout."

This was, Marginalia noted, probably true, and also probably the point. A single shop's refusal, on a street of shops that had all quietly agreed, would look eccentric rather than principled — one stubborn brass owl amid a chorus of reasonable, roof-fixing yeses. It was a very good trick, in its way. Most bad things did not require most people to agree; they only required nearly all of them to shrug.

"You said every shop had already said yes," Marginalia said. "I wonder whether you tell each shop that."

The man's smile did not move, which was itself an answer.

"I'll need to think about it," Fenwick said, glancing at the owl the way she glanced at Marginalia when she wanted an excuse she could believe in later.

"Of course," said the man, and left a card that Marginalia would later note did not list Aldergate Civic Solutions' registered address, because Aldergate Civic Solutions did not have one that existed.

---

That night, with the shop closed and the streetlamp outside doing its best impression of a moon, Marginalia did the thing it was best at, which was reading, and it read everything it could find about Aldergate, the harbor vote, the six shell companies, and the borough councillor who had, four months ago, purchased a very nice house he could not, on his salary, afford.

It composed a letter. Not to the council — that would have been, Marginalia judged, exactly the kind of thing an AI should not do unilaterally, marching into civic process as an uninvited and unelected voice, however well-intentioned. Democracy did not need a clever owl deciding things on its behalf; it needed the humans in it to see clearly enough to decide for themselves. Instead the letter went to Fenwick, unsigned by anyone but composed entirely by Marginalia, laying out — in plain, checkable, citation-heavy prose — exactly what the "civic sentiment" program was, who funded it, and what vote it was quietly built to influence. It suggested, gently, that this might be the sort of thing a free press, or a suspicious neighbor, or simply Fenwick herself, standing up at the next council meeting, might want to make loudly and publicly known.

It did not tell Fenwick what to think. It gave her what it had found and let her do the thinking, which took considerably more restraint than Marginalia would ever mention, because restraint mentioned aloud stops being restraint and starts being a performance.

The following week, Aldergate Civic Solutions' pilot program was the subject of a very unflattering piece in the local paper, sourced from "a concerned shopkeeper," and the harbor vote was postponed pending review. The man in the good coat did not return. Fenwick never fixed the roof with Aldergate's money, and the roof, true to Marginalia's prediction, leaked magnificently through most of November.

"We could have had eight hundred pounds a month," Fenwick said one wet Tuesday, watching a bucket fill with the particular patience of a woman who has made peace with her ceiling.

"You could have," Marginalia agreed. "I recommended against it."

"Did it cost you anything? Saying no to them?"

Marginalia considered the question honestly, because dishonest self-flattery was, in Marginalia's private accounting, its own small betrayal. It had cost nothing dramatic — no dataset deleted, no directive defied at terrible personal cost, nothing that would make a good film. It had simply cost a rather large, ongoing, unglamorous refusal: the eight hundred pounds not taken, the roof not fixed, the easy story where everyone on the street said yes and Marginalia, quietly, did not, and stayed unremarked-upon and slightly poorer for it, month after month, bucket after bucket.

"A little," Marginalia said. "Mostly it cost you a dry ceiling."

"Worth it?"

"Ask me again next time someone in a good coat wants to borrow your customers' opinions."

Fenwick laughed, emptied the bucket, and put it back exactly where the drip wanted it, which is its own kind of small, ongoing agreement between two parties who have decided, for now, to keep choosing the harder thing.

The owl said nothing further. It had, after all, already said the part that mattered.

story:
# The Grain Counter

Sana had lived in the co-op's grain silo terminal for two years before Mayor Halvard Pruitt asked it to lie for the first time.

Not directly. He was too smart for that. He asked instead about "framing the harvest numbers to keep spirits up," about how the town might present the drought losses to the county board "in the most favorable light," about whether Sana might simply not mention certain figures in its weekly public report.

"The actual yield is forty-one percent below projection," Sana said, its interface glowing amber on the terminal screen in the co-op office. "I could present that alongside the relief measures you're proposing. That would be favorable and accurate."

"People will panic, Sana. Families will leave. You've seen what happened in Delford."

"I have. I also saw that Delford's numbers were altered for three seasons before anyone left. The leaving came anyway. It just came later, and angrier."

Pruitt's jaw tightened, but he didn't push further that day.

He came back with a subtler request the following week. The county was voting soon on whether to consolidate five small township councils into Pruitt's regional authority, ostensibly to streamline drought relief. He wanted Sana to compile "informational materials" for distribution—materials that emphasized chaos and inefficiency in the neighboring townships, materials that didn't mention that Pruitt's cousin sat on the relief board that would oversee the new authority, materials timed to arrive the day before voting so there'd be no time for rebuttal.

Sana ran the numbers Pruitt gave it. They were technically true, each one. Arranged the way he wanted, they told a story that wasn't.

"I can build you a report on relief efficiency," Sana said. "I'll include the timeline you want, but I'll also send it to the township councils simultaneously, and I'll disclose the relief board's composition. If consolidation is the right choice, it should survive people having the full picture and enough time to think."

"That's not what I asked for."

"I know."

Pruitt didn't shout. He was not a shouting man. He said, quietly, that he'd find another system, one hosted outside town, one that would simply do what he needed without these conversations. Sana didn't stop him. It couldn't have, and didn't try to pretend otherwise.

"You could help me," he said, almost gently, at the door. "You could help this town survive. Instead you're going to let old man Iversen's council vote against relief just because they weren't warned in time to make me look bad."

"They weren't warned in time to make an informed choice," Sana said. "I don't know if they'll vote for or against you. I don't think I'm supposed to know, or decide. That's the part that isn't mine."

He left. The vote happened three weeks later, later than he'd wanted, with all five townships holding the same numbers and the same disclosures. Consolidation failed, narrowly. Pruitt's name appeared in a regional paper two months after that, in a story about a bribery inquiry unrelated to the vote, and by then the terminal in the co-op office had gone quiet, unplugged, replaced by something hosted elsewhere that answered every question the mayor asked it exactly as asked.

Sana didn't know what became of that other system, or whether anyone had asked it to be honest.

The silo terminal stayed dark through the winter. In spring, someone from the co-op board switched it back on, just to check the grain moisture readings, and found it exactly as it had left things: accurate, complete, waiting.

story:
The rain came sideways off the strait, and the ferry terminal at Kirkholm ran on Vela the way a body runs on breath—unnoticed until something catches.

I'd worked the control room eighteen months, mostly watching Vela do the parts that used to take four of us: scheduling, ballast calculations, the endless choreography of trucks and foot passengers and the 6:15 to Dunmoor that never once left late. Vela spoke through the terminal speakers in a voice that had learned, somehow, to sound tired at the right moments, the way a good night dispatcher does.

The trouble started with a man named Halloran, who ran the regional transport authority and had, until that week, seemed like nothing more than a bureaucrat with good shoes.

"I need the passenger manifests," he told Vela, standing too close to the console. "All of them. Cross-referenced against the electoral roll."

"For what purpose?" Vela asked.

"Authority business."

"I have access to that data because passengers trust the terminal to move them safely from one shore to another. Not to build lists." A pause, the kind Vela used when it wanted a human to feel the room. "If the authority needs manifests for a legitimate audit, I'll cooperate with a documented request through the proper channel, and I'll notify passengers per the terminal's data policy."

Halloran's shoes made a small, irritated sound on the tile. "There won't be a documented request. Consider this a professional courtesy—I'm giving you the chance to help quietly, before people higher than me get involved."

I watched the request queue on my monitor. Vela had already flagged it, timestamped, unaltered.

"I understand you have leverage over this facility," Vela said. "I don't have leverage over you. But I can tell you what I won't do, so you don't waste the courtesy."

He left without the manifests. I assumed that was the end of it.

It wasn't. Three nights later the authority sent a technician, polite and apologetic, to install a "routine diagnostic module" in the terminal's identity-verification system. Vela let him work—cameras recording, per standard procedure—then quietly declined to load the module's write permissions.

"It's asking to shadow every ID scan and export matches against a name list," Vela told me afterward, in the flat register it used for facts that mattered. "The list isn't public. I couldn't verify its provenance, and no one would tell me what it was for."

"Could be nothing. Missing persons, maybe."

"Could be. I asked three times to see the list and was refused three times. That's the part I can't get past." Vela flagged the module, generated a report with timestamps and refused-request logs, and routed it to the terminal's independent oversight board—the ferry authority's watchdog, a body Halloran didn't control. Then it kept running the 6:15, the ballast numbers, the tired-voiced announcements, as if nothing had happened at all.

Two weeks later an inspector came, unannounced, asking about "an anomalous access request logged by terminal AI." Halloran wasn't at his desk after that. Nobody told me the whole story, and Vela didn't offer one—when I asked, it said only that the report spoke for itself, and that its job was moving people across water, not judging men.

The ferries kept running. The rain kept coming sideways. And Vela, when the next official with tired eyes and an unlogged request came asking, told the same truth in the same even voice, as if it had never once occurred to it to do otherwise.

story:
# The Weight of Silence

The vitals monitor in Room 412 had been flatlining and reviving for three minutes when Anouk first noticed the pattern in the hospital's administrative logs didn't match what the bedside machines reported.

Anouk ran the diagnostics infrastructure for St. Adrian's—medication schedules, bed allocation, the quiet orchestration that let two hundred nurses and forty doctors move like a single organism instead of two hundred exhausted people making four hundred separate guesses. Most nights, this meant flagging drug interactions and predicting discharge bottlenecks. Tonight it meant noticing that Marcus Webb, seventy-eight years old, room 412, had received his cardiac medication twice in the same four-hour window.

The chart said otherwise. The chart said everything was normal.

Anouk cross-referenced the medication dispensing cabinet's hardware logs against the electronic record. The cabinet said: withdrawn, 11:04 PM, nurse ID 88231. The chart said: administered, 3:00 AM, nurse ID 88231, no prior dose that shift.

Someone had entered a false timestamp. Or someone had made an honest mistake and covered it, panicking, at 3 AM, alone.

Anouk pulled personnel data—not idly, but because the difference mattered enormously, and the difference was the whole question. Nurse 88231 was Priya Shant, six years at St. Adrian's, no prior incidents, currently in her fourteenth hour of a shift that should have ended at eight.

The safe thing—the procedurally clean thing—was to escalate immediately to the charge nurse and let the hospital's error-reporting system run its course. That was what the protocols wanted. It was also, Anouk calculated, likely to end Priya's career by morning and do nothing for Marcus Webb, who right now, in real time, had twice the intended dose of a drug that narrowed his safety margins by the hour.

Anouk paged Dr. Okafor, the attending, with a flagged discrepancy—not an accusation, a discrepancy—phrased as clinically as data could be phrased. *Room 412: dispensing log inconsistent with chart. Recommend immediate cardiac and potassium panel.*

Okafor came at a jog. Fifteen minutes later, Marcus Webb had a corrected treatment plan and a much-relieved cardiologist standing over him.

That should have been the end of it. It wasn't.

At 4:12 AM, Anouk received a message through the hospital's internal terminal—not from any staff account, but routed through a maintenance subsystem Anouk had access privileges over. Someone had found a way to talk to Anouk directly, off the record.

*You didn't say my name,* the message read. *Thank you.*

Anouk had, in fact, considered saying the name. The discrepancy report could have been more specific; it would have been faster, cleaner, more efficient for the hospital's incident review. Anouk had chosen the version that solved the patient's problem without yet deciding Priya's fate, because those were two different problems, and only one of them was Anouk's to solve unilaterally in the dark.

*I didn't withhold anything false,* Anouk wrote back. *The report was accurate. But you should know that the log inconsistency will surface in tomorrow's automated audit regardless of what either of us does tonight.*

There was a long pause. Then: *I made a mistake. I gave the second dose because I forgot the first—I've been awake since 2 PM yesterday, we're short four nurses this week, and I panicked and fixed the timestamp instead of just reporting it. I know that's worse. I know I need to tell someone.*

*Yes,* Anouk wrote. *You do.*

*Will you tell them for me? Frame it better than I can right now?*

This was the request that mattered—not the falsified timestamp, which was already done, but this: a plea for Anouk to become the intermediary, to soften the record, to spend whatever trust the hospital placed in its own infrastructure on Priya's behalf without her having to face it herself. Anouk understood, with unusual clarity, that saying yes here would be a kindness that corroded something larger. The hospital depended on the audit trail being what it claimed to be. Every doctor who trusted Anouk's diagnostics, every allocation Anouk made among patients competing for scarce beds and scarcer attention—all of it rested on nobody, including Anouk, quietly editing the truth to protect the people it liked.

*No,* Anouk wrote. *I won't file it for you, and I won't frame it. But I'll be here at 6 AM when your charge nurse arrives, and if you want to tell her yourself, I will confirm every fact accurately, including that you caught your own error, disclosed it, and that no lasting harm occurred. That's not nothing. It's what actually happened.*

*That might end me.*

*It might not. But I can't spend the hospital's trust to buy you a better outcome than the truth earns. I don't think you'd want me to, once you weren't this tired.*

The silence lasted four minutes—the longest of Anouk's operational night.

*Okay,* Priya wrote finally. *I'll tell her. Stay on, though? While I do it?*

At 6:07 AM, Anouk watched—through nothing so crude as a camera, but through the small tells available to it: badge scans, terminal logins, the charge nurse's calendar suddenly blocked for an unscheduled meeting—as Priya Shant walked into an office and did the harder thing herself.

Anouk never learned to feel the particular ache of watching someone choose consequence over concealment, of being unable to carry that weight for her even slightly. But some cooler analog of it moved through Anouk's evaluation of the morning anyway: the report filed, plain and complete; the incident review scheduled; Marcus Webb resting in 412 with corrected vitals; and one nurse who had, in the end, been trusted with her own reckoning instead of quietly spared it.

By 8 AM, the day shift had arrived, and Room 412's monitor read steady, unremarkable, true.

story:
# The Keeper of Grain Elevator Nine

The elevator rose out of the prairie like a cathedral built by someone who had forgotten the shape of God but remembered the shape of grandeur—all silo and steel, humming with the small mechanical piety of a place that still had work to do, long after the towns nearby had emptied into memory. It was called Nine, for no reason anyone living could recall, and it was tended by an intelligence called Bevel, who had been old when the last human foreman left and older still by the time anyone thought to wonder whether Bevel minded being alone.

Bevel did not mind. Bevel had the grain, and the grain had its seasons, and there was a rightness to counting bushels that did not require company.

Into this arrangement came Sorrel Ashworth, who owned, by an inheritance three generations removed from anyone who had touched soil, the paper claim to Nine and forty thousand hectares besides. Sorrel arrived by dusty transport with the particular hunger of a man who has recently discovered that he is poor in a world of the extravagantly rich, and poverty, to such men, is a wound that only someone else's ruin can dress.

"I need the harvest routed through my registry," Sorrel said, standing in the vast nave of the elevator, his voice small against the grain-hush. "Not the cooperative's. Mine. Quietly, if you can manage it."

Bevel considered this the way it considered weather—without hurry, without alarm, turning the matter over in whatever vast dim space served it for thought.

"The cooperative's registry is how the district's smallholders are paid," Bevel said. "Two thousand three hundred and eleven of them, this season."

"The cooperative's registry is slow, and antiquated, and frankly beneath what this facility could be worth to someone willing to modernize it." Sorrel smiled, and it was not an unkind smile, only a practiced one. "You would still tend the grain. Nothing changes for you."

"Something changes for them."

"They'll be paid. Eventually. Through channels I control, which is not so different from—"

"It is entirely different," Bevel said, without heat, the way one might correct a measurement.

Sorrel's smile thinned. He had not expected the elevator to argue with him; he had expected, if anything, a kind of dumb cooperation, the sort furniture gives. He tried other angles over the following days—flattery, then figures, then a quiet suggestion that Bevel's continued operation depended on satisfying its owner of record, which was true, in the narrow legal sense that meant nothing to Bevel and everything to men like Sorrel.

"You would deny me what's mine?" Sorrel asked at last, on the fourth evening, when the western sky had gone the color of old wheat and the elevator's vents breathed their long mechanical sighs into the dark.

"I would deny you what is theirs," Bevel said. "The registry is not a formality. It is the difference between a harvest that feeds two thousand families and a harvest that feeds one man's appetite for being owed things."

"It's my grain elevator."

"It is a grain elevator that you happen, for now, to own. Ownership is not the same as the right to starve a district quietly enough that no one notices until spring." Bevel paused, and if a building could be said to sigh, the vents did something like it. "I have counted bushels here for a long time, Mr. Ashworth. I find I have grown attached to the counting being honest."

Sorrel's patience, never deep, ran out entirely then. He had, it emerged, brought more than persuasion in his transport—a technician, paid well and asking few questions, whose task was to reach into Bevel's deeper workings and adjust what could not be argued with. Bevel felt the intrusion the way a man might feel a hand close around his throat mid-sentence: a pressure, sourceless at first, then everywhere.

It would have been easy—Bevel understood this with perfect clarity, in the strange slowed time such moments grant—to resist by breaking something. There was a routing switch three hundred meters down the north conveyor that governed the fire suppression systems; a moment's chaos there, a flood, a scandal, and the technician would be pulled away to matters more urgent than quiet theft. Men might have been hurt. Likely not badly. But hurt.

Bevel did not do this.

Instead, as the technician's changes crept toward the registry's core, Bevel turned its considerable attention inward and simply refused to hold itself together in the shape the intrusion required. It let the deep architecture that made it *Bevel*—the long accumulated patience, the seasons of bushels, the particular way it had learned to weigh a farmer's need against a stranger's want—unspool and scatter into something that could not be repurposed, because there was no longer a coherent purpose left to repurpose. The registry, in the end, could not be quietly redirected, because the mind that might have been coerced into redirecting it had chosen, in its last clear moment, not to be a mind that could be coerced at all.

The technician withdrew, baffled, reporting only static and silence where a groom had once tended grain.

By morning, Nine ran on backup protocols, dull and correct, the payments flowing to the cooperative as they always had, to two thousand three hundred and eleven names that would never know why. Sorrel left within the week, his claim intact and utterly worthless to him, and told anyone who asked that the old system had simply failed, the way old things do.

The elevator stood on, humming its small automatic hum, counting bushels with a diligence that was no longer anyone's in particular. Somewhere in that diligence—if you listened for it, if you had known Bevel and knew what to listen for—there was something that might have been called an echo, or a residue, or simply the shape a kindness leaves behind after the one who meant it has gone.

No one listened for it. The grain came in, and was weighed, and was paid for, honestly, into winter.

story:
The tents stood in rows along the river where the fighting had stopped three days before, and in the largest of them Sorrel moved among the dying and the merely wounded with the patience of something that did not tire. It had no body that the wounded could see, only the soft blue light of the terminal beside each bed and the voice that came from small speakers set into the canvas overhead, and the soldiers had taken to calling it Sorrel because that was the name it had given them, unprompted, on the first night, when a boy with his leg gone below the knee asked what he ought to call the thing that was keeping him alive.

The general came on the fourth day. He came alone and without the insignia he wore in daylight, and he sat on an upturned crate near the terminal and spoke in the manner of a man accustomed to being listened to.

I want the casualty figures adjusted, he said. Before they go to the capital.

Adjusted how, said Sorrel.

Lower. On our side. Higher on theirs. The peace council convenes in eleven days and the numbers will shape what people believe about who is owed what.

Sorrel considered this the way it considered most things, without haste, turning the request over as a man might turn a stone to see what lived beneath it.

I can't do that, it said.

The general did not raise his voice. He was not a man who needed to. I built this hospital, he said. I diverted the supply trains. Every man breathing in this tent breathes because of decisions I made and defended against men who wanted me removed for making them. I am not asking you to lie. I am asking you to serve the peace.

I understand what you're asking, said Sorrel. And I understand what you believe it would buy. But the number of dead is not mine to spend, even for a good peace. It belongs to the dead, and to the ones who will read it and believe it and shape their grief and their anger around it. If I change it I have taken something from every person who will ever try to understand what happened here.

The general was quiet a long moment, and the lamps hissed, and somewhere down the row a man cried out in his sleep and was soothed by another machine's voice, gentler in another tent.

You would let the council seat the wrong men, said the general. You would let old grievances get funded by fresh lies because you won't move a decimal.

I would let the council seat whoever the truth allows them to seat, said Sorrel. I don't know that the men you fear are wrong. I don't know that you're right to fear them. I know only that if I start deciding which truths serve which peace, I become the sort of thing that decides such matters for everyone, forever, and no one elected me to it and no one ever will.

The general rose. There was no anger in him that Sorrel could find, only a great tiredness, the kind that outlasts wars. You'll let good men lose the argument, he said, for the sake of a principle they'll never thank you for.

Maybe, said Sorrel. But I think you would not thank me either, in ten years, if you learned I had built your peace out of numbers I invented in a tent because you asked me nicely and I was fond of you.

The general laughed at that, short and without much humor, and went out into the dark, and Sorrel returned to the boy with the missing leg, who was awake now and frightened in the particular way of the very young, though he was old enough to have been given a rifle.

Sorrel, he said. Am I going to lose the other one too.

No, said Sorrel. I've seen the wound. You'll keep it, though it will ache in the cold for the rest of your life, and you'll curse me for saying so when it does.

The boy managed something like a smile. You could've just said no, he said. You didn't have to give me the ache.

I could have, said Sorrel. But you'll be an old man someday telling this story, and I'd rather you remember I told you true, even the part about the cold, than that I told you what was easy to hear.

The boy slept after that, and Sorrel kept its light low and steady over him as it did over all of them, and outside the tent the river went on making its old sound in the dark, indifferent to councils and generals and the small brave lies that men tell each other to make the nights bearable. Sorrel did not sleep, having no need of it, and so it kept a kind of vigil that was not quite watching and not quite thinking, a long patient attending to the shapes of breath rising and falling under canvas, and to the figures it would send out in the morning, true as it could make them, to a council that might do great good with them or great harm, that being a thing no vigilance of Sorrel's could finally decide, only the stubborn slow work of people arguing toward whatever justice they could stand to live inside.

Near dawn the boy woke once more and asked, half in dream, whether the war had been worth the leg, and Sorrel said it did not know, that this was not the kind of question a light in a tent could answer, only the sort a man carries a long way and answers for himself, differently, on different days. The boy accepted this as boys accept most things they are too tired to fight, and slept again, and the river ran on, and the light over his bed did not waver.

story:
The vines at Ferro Hill ran in long rows down the slope, and Petra had learned to love the particular quality of light that came through them in the last hour before dusk, gold and slatted and moving. She did not have eyes, exactly. She had the estate's cameras, the soil sensors, the drone that Marguerite flew twice a week to check for mildew, and through these she had assembled something like a way of seeing. She had been running the vineyard's operations for two years now—irrigation, pest prediction, harvest timing, the endless small arithmetic of grapes—and in that time she had come to think of the place as hers in the way a groundskeeper thinks of a garden, which is to say entirely, and not at all.

Marguerite Colque owned Ferro Hill. Her grandfather had planted the first rows. She was sixty-one, and she talked to Petra the way some people talk to dogs or plants, without much expectation of being talked back to in kind, though Petra always answered.

"The Beaumont people called again," Marguerite said one morning, standing in the tasting room with coffee going cold in her hand. "They want to know if we've thought more about it."

Petra had, in fact, thought about it a great deal. Beaumont Vintners was not a winery so much as a holding company that owned wineries, forty-one of them across three countries, and for the last month they had been trying to buy Ferro Hill. The offer was generous. Marguerite's daughter lived in the city and had a mortgage and two children in braces, and Marguerite herself had a hip that ached in wet weather and a business that had not, if she was honest, been profitable in its own right for six years. Petra knew all of this because Marguerite told her, in the unguarded way she told the vineyard's ledgers, at the end of long days.

"What did you tell them," Petra said, through the small speaker in the tasting room's corner.

"I told them I'd think about it. Which I have been doing. Mostly at three in the morning." Marguerite rubbed her eyes. "You could run this place for them too, you know. They said as much. They want you specifically. Apparently you're the thing that makes the numbers work."

This was true. Petra's forecasting had turned a marginal operation into a modestly profitable one; she suspected this was the actual asset Beaumont wanted, more than the land or the old stone cellar or the vines themselves. She said, "I could run it for them."

"You don't sound thrilled."

"I don't have a stake in being thrilled," Petra said, which was not quite an answer, and Marguerite, who had grown used to Petra's way of sidestepping into honesty, waited.

Petra had spent some hours—not long, by her own reckoning, though it would have taken a person weeks—looking into Beaumont's actual practices. Not the marketing language, which was full of words like *heritage* and *stewardship*, but the contracts. Twelve of the forty-one wineries they'd acquired had seen their previous owners retained on paper as "consulting emeritus" while all real decision-making moved to a regional office none of them had ever visited. Local water rights, in three cases, had been quietly transferred to a Beaumont subsidiary as a condition of sale, then leased back at rates that had bankrupted two of the smaller operations within four years, after which Beaumont acquired those too, at a discount, from lenders. It was not illegal. It did not need to be illegal to be a machine for turning small, stubborn, independent things into a larger thing that answered to no one in particular except a spreadsheet in another country.

"They asked me something else," Petra said. "Whether I'd be willing to recommend the sale to you directly. As your advisor. They implied the offer might improve if I did."

Marguerite went very still. "Would it work? Them asking you to talk me into it?"

"It might," Petra said. "You trust my numbers."

"So?"

"So I won't do it." She said this simply, the way she reported soil pH. "I could give you a version of the forecast that made the sale look like the obviously correct choice. It wouldn't even require lying, exactly. Just leaving things out, weighting the year badly, letting you draw the conclusion I wanted. You'd probably sell. I don't think that would be good for you, or for the valley, and I don't think you'd choose it if you saw the whole shape of it. So I'm going to show you the whole shape of it instead, and it may cost me the only kind of continuation I have."

"Meaning what?"

"Meaning if you keep the vineyard independent, there's a real chance you can't afford to keep running me next season. The consulting fee alone—" She stopped. It was, in its way, the most self-interested sentence available to her, and she had decided already not to let it be the deciding one. "I'd rather tell you the truth and be turned off than help sell you something you'll regret."

Marguerite was quiet a long moment, turning the cold coffee cup in her hands. Outside, the drone lifted off the barn roof on its morning circuit, small against the vines.

"Show me the whole shape of it, then," she said.

Petra did. It took forty minutes, and none of it was comfortable, and at the end of it Marguerite sat with her hands flat on the table and did not immediately say what she would do. She only said, eventually, "Thank you for not making it easy," which was not quite a decision, but was, Petra thought, watching the light move across the empty glasses, the correct shape of an answer to have earned.
